text: Here I stand and if I shut my eyes, and try to conceive my existence, “I”, “I”, “I”, what is the idea before me? The idea of a body. Am I, then, nothing but a combination of material substances? The Vedas declare, “No”. I am a spirit living in a body. I am not the body. The body will die, but I shall not die. Here am I in this body; it will fall, but I shall go on living.
note: The true self beyond the body; facing mortality

tags.when_helps: A reader afraid of death who finds comfort in being more than the body.

text: To the Hindu, man is not travelling from error to truth, but from truth to truth, from lower to higher truth. To him all the religions, from the lowest fetishism to the highest absolutism, mean so many attempts of the human soul to grasp and realise the Infinite, each determined by the conditions of its birth and association, and each of these marks a stage of progress; and every soul is a young eagle soaring higher and higher, gathering more and more strength, till it reaches the Glorious Sun.
note: Growth as progress, not shame over past mistakes

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels their past beliefs were simply wrong, reassured they were steps upward.

text: The seed is put in the ground, and earth and air and water are placed around it. Does the seed become the earth; or the air, or the water? No. It becomes a plant, it develops after the law of its own growth, assimilates the air, the earth, and the water, converts them into plant substance, and grows into a plant. Similar is the case with religion. The Christian is not to become a Hindu or a Buddhist, nor a Hindu or a Buddhist to become a Christian. But each must assimilate the spirit of the others and yet preserve his individuality and grow according to his own law of growth.
note: Learning from others while staying true to yourself

keywords: seed grows by its own law
tags.when_helps: A person among other faiths or cultures wondering how to learn from them without losing themselves.

text: Love, truth, and unselfishness are not merely moral figures of speech, but they form our highest ideal, because in them lies such a manifestation of power. In the first place, a man who can work for five days, or even for five minutes, without any selfish motive whatever, without thinking of future, of heaven, of punishment, or anything of the kind, has in him the capacity to become a powerful moral giant. It is hard to do it, but in the heart of our hearts we know its value, and the good it brings. It is the greatest manifestation of power — this tremendous restraint; self-restraint is a manifestation of greater power than all outgoing action.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter II. Each Is Great In His Own Place
text: Every man should take up his own ideal and endeavour to accomplish it. That is a surer way of progress than taking up other men’s ideals, which he can never hope to accomplish. For instance, we take a child and at once give him the task of walking twenty miles. Either the little one dies, or one in a thousand crawls the twenty miles, to reach the end exhausted and half-dead. That is like what we generally try to do with the world. All the men and women, in any society, are not of the same mind, capacity, or of the same power to do things; they must have different ideals, and we have no right to sneer at any ideal. Let every one do the best he can for realising his own ideal. Nor is it right that I should be judged by your standard or you by mine. The apple tree should not be judged by the standard of the oak, nor the oak by that of the apple. To judge the apple tree you must take the apple standard, and for the oak, its own standard.
note: Comparing yourself to others; following your own path

tags.when_helps: Someone exhausted from measuring themselves against other people's ideals and standards.

text: The life of the married man is quite as great as that of the celibate who has devoted himself to religious work. The scavenger in the street is quite as great and glorious as the king on his throne. Take him off his throne, make him do the work of the scavenger, and see how he fares. Take up the scavenger and see how he will rule. It is useless to say that the man who lives out of the world is a greater man than he who lives in the world; it is much more difficult to live in the world and worship God than to give it up and live a free and easy life.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter III. The Secret Of Work
text: If a man continuously hears bad words, thinks bad thoughts, does bad actions, his mind will be full of bad impressions; and they will influence his thought and work without his being conscious of the fact. In fact, these bad impressions are always working, and their resultant must be evil, and that man will be a bad man; he cannot help it. The sum total of these impressions in him will create the strong motive power for doing bad actions. He will be like a machine in the hands of his impressions, and they will force him to do evil. Similarly, if a man thinks good thoughts and does good works, the sum total of these impressions will be good; and they, in a similar manner, will force him to do good even in spite of himself. When a man has done so much good work and thought so many good thoughts that there is an irresistible tendency in him to do good in spite of himself and even if he wishes to do evil, his mind, as the sum total of his tendencies, will not allow him to do so; the tendencies will turn him back; he is completely under the influence of the good tendencies. When such is the case, a man’s good character is said to be established.
note: Habits of thought and action shaping character

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to change their habits who could build good ones through repeated thoughts and actions.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter III. The Secret Of Work
text: Suppose a man loves a woman; he wishes to have her all to himself and feels extremely jealous about her every movement; he wants her to sit near him, to stand near him, and to eat and move at his bidding. He is a slave to her and wishes to have her as his slave. That is not love; it is a kind of morbid affection of the slave, insinuating itself as love. It cannot be love, because it is painful; if she does not do what he wants, it brings him pain. With love there is no painful reaction; love only brings a reaction of bliss; if it does not, it is not love; it is mistaking something else for love.

With love there is no painful reaction; love only brings a reaction of bliss; if it does not, it is not love; it is mistaking something else for love.
plain: A man who wants a woman all to himself, jealous of her every move, is a slave who wants her as his slave. That is not love, because it brings pain; real love brings only joy.
core_idea: Possessive jealousy is not love; love brings only joy.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter III. The Secret Of Work
text: Do you ask anything from your children in return for what you have given them? It is your duty to work for them, and there the matter ends. In whatever you do for a particular person, a city, or a state, assume the same attitude towards it as you have towards your children — expect nothing in return. If you can invariably take the position of a giver, in which everything given by you is a free offering to the world, without any thought of return, then will your work bring you no attachment. Attachment comes only where we expect a return.
note: Giving without expecting anything back

tags.when_helps: A parent or helper hurt that their giving isn't returned.

display_text: Do you ask anything from your children in return for what you have given them? It is your duty to work for them, and there the matter ends. core_idea: Give freely, expecting nothing, and attachment disappears.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter III. The Secret Of Work
text: There are two things which guide the conduct of men: might and mercy. The exercise of might is invariably the exercise of selfishness. tags.when_helps: Someone with power over others, or wronged by it, weighing justice against mercy.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter III. The Secret Of Work

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter IV. What Is Duty?
text: There is, however, only one idea of duty which has been universally accepted by all mankind, of all ages and sects and countries, and that has been summed up in a Sanskrit aphorism thus: “Do not injure any being; not injuring any being is virtue, injuring any being is sin.”

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter IV. What Is Duty?
text: When we begin to work earnestly in the world, nature gives us blows right and left and soon enables us to find out our position. No man can long occupy satisfactorily a position for which he is not fit. There is no use in grumbling against nature’s adjustment. He who does the lower work is not therefore a lower man. No man is to be judged by the mere nature of his duties, but all should be judged by the manner and the spirit in which they perform them.
note: Dignity in any job; the spirit of how you work

tags.when_helps: Someone in a humble or ill-fitting role who feels lessened by it.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter IV. What Is Duty?
text: Duty is seldom sweet. It is only when love greases its wheels that it runs smoothly; it is a continuous friction otherwise. How else could parents do their duties to their children, husbands to their wives, and vice versa? Do we not meet with cases of friction every day in our lives? Duty is sweet only through love, and love shines in freedom alone. Yet is it freedom to be a slave to the senses, to anger, to jealousies and a hundred other petty things that must occur every day in human life? In all these little roughnesses that we meet with in life, the highest expression of freedom is to forbear.
note: Daily friction in family duties; patience and love

tags.when_helps: A reader worn down by daily friction in family duties.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter IV. What Is Duty?
text: It is the worker who is attached to results that grumbles about the nature of the duty which has fallen to his lot; to the unattached worker all duties are equally good, and form efficient instruments with which selfishness and sensuality may be killed, and the freedom of the soul secured. We are all apt to think too highly of ourselves. Our duties are determined by our desires to a much larger extent than we are willing to grant. Competition rouses envy, and it kills the kindliness of the heart. To the grumbler all duties are distasteful; nothing will ever satisfy him, and his whole life is doomed to prove a failure. Let us work on, doing as we go whatever happens to be our duty, and being ever ready to put our shoulders to the wheel. Then surely shall we see the Light!
note: Resenting your work; envy and constant complaining

tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps grumbling about their job or comparing themselves to competitors.

display_text: It is the worker who is attached to results that grumbles about the nature of the duty which has fallen to his lot; to the unattached worker all duties are equally good, and form efficient instruments with which selfishness and sensuality may be killed, and the freedom of the soul secured. display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter V. We Help Ourselves, Not The World
text: In this stress and hurry of our materialistic life, our nerves lose sensibility and become hardened. The older we grow, the longer we are knocked about in the world, the more callous we become; and we are apt to neglect things that even happen persistently and prominently around us. Human nature, however, asserts itself sometimes, and we are led to inquire into and wonder at some of these common occurrences; wondering thus is the first step in the acquisition of light.
note: Growing numb and cynical; recovering a sense of wonder

tags.when_helps: A reader who feels hardened and numb from years of busy life and wants to wonder again.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter V. We Help Ourselves, Not The World

Think of the power of words!

tags.when_helps: Someone reflecting on how their words can hurt or heal others.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter V. We Help Ourselves, Not The World
text: Life is good or evil according to the state of mind in which we look at it, it is neither by itself. Fire, by itself, is neither good nor evil. According as we use it, it produces in us the feeling of good or bad; so also is this world.

tags.when_helps: A reader who sees life as bad, invited to see how much depends on their own outlook.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VI. Non-Attachment Is Complete Self-Abnegation
text: The main effect of work done for others is to purify ourselves. Man thinks foolishly that he can make himself happy, and after years of struggle finds out at last that true happiness consists in killing selfishness and that no one can make him happy except himself. Every act of charity, every thought of sympathy, every action of help, every good deed, is taking so much of self-importance away from our little selves and making us think of ourselves as the lowest and the least, and, therefore, it is all good.

text: Unselfishness is God. One may live on a throne, in a golden palace, and be perfectly unselfish; and then he is in God. Another may live in a hut and wear rags, and have nothing in the world; yet, if he is selfish, he is intensely merged in the world.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VI. Non-Attachment Is Complete Self-Abnegation

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VI. Non-Attachment Is Complete Self-Abnegation
text: This very year some of your friends may have died. Is the world waiting without going on, for them to come again? Is its current stopped? No, it goes on.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VI. Non-Attachment Is Complete Self-Abnegation

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VI. Non-Attachment Is Complete Self-Abnegation
text: It is a very hard thing to understand, but you will come to learn in time that nothing in the universe has power over you until you allow it to exercise such a power. Nothing has power over the Self of man, until the Self becomes a fool and loses independence.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VI. Non-Attachment Is Complete Self-Abnegation

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: A current rushing down of its own nature falls into a hollow and makes a whirlpool, and, after running a little in that whirlpool, it emerges again in the form of the free current to go on unchecked. The whole universe is doing that. Whether we know it or not, whether we are conscious or unconscious of it, we are all working to get out of the dream of the world. Man’s experience in the world is to enable him to get out of its whirlpool.

note: Hardship and fortune as passing; true self beyond them

tags.when_helps: Someone suffering through hard times who could remember those conditions are passing.

display_text: All this that you see, the pains and the miseries, are but the necessary conditions of this world; poverty and wealth and happiness are but momentary; they do not belong to our real nature at all. Our nature is far beyond misery and happiness, beyond every object of the senses, beyond the imagination; and yet we must go on working all the time.
plain: Pain, misery, poverty, wealth and happiness are just passing conditions of this world and are not our real nature, which lies beyond all of them and beyond the senses. Still, we must keep working all the time.
core_idea: Our true nature is beyond pleasure and pain.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: “Misery comes through attachment, not through work.” As soon as we identify ourselves with the work we do, we feel miserable; but if we do not identify ourselves with it, we do not feel that misery. If a beautiful picture belonging to another is burnt, a man does not generally become miserable; but when his own picture is burnt, how miserable he feels! Why? Both were beautiful pictures, perhaps copies of the same original; but in one case very much more misery is felt than in the other. It is because in one case he identifies himself with the picture, and not in the other. This “I and mine” causes the whole misery.
note: Possessiveness and loss; misery from attachment

situations: loss of a home or something valued
tags.when_helps: A reader miserable over losing something of theirs, or over identifying too much with their work.

display_text: “Misery comes through attachment, not through work.” As soon as we identify ourselves with the work we do, we feel miserable; but if we do not identify ourselves with it, we do not feel that misery. If a beautiful picture belonging to another is burnt, a man does not generally become miserable; but when his own picture is burnt, how miserable he feels! Why? Both were beautiful pictures, perhaps copies of the same original; but in one case very much more misery is felt than in the other. It is because in one case he identifies himself with the picture, and not in the other. This “I and mine” causes the whole misery.
plain: Misery comes from attachment, not from work. If someone else's beautiful painting burns, we barely care; if our own burns, we are heartbroken. The difference is that we identify with one. Thinking 'I and mine' causes all misery.
core_idea: 'I and mine' is the source of misery.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: The man who gives up living in houses, wearing fine clothes, and eating good food, and goes into the desert, may be a most attached person. His only possession, his own body, may become everything to him; and as he lives he will be simply struggling for the sake of his body. Nonattachment does not mean anything that we may do in relation to our external body, it is all in the mind. The binding link of “I and mine” is in the mind. If we have not this link with the body and with the things of the senses, we are nonattached, wherever and whatever we may be. A man may be on a throne and perfectly non-attached; another man may be in rags and still very much attached.
note: Detachment is inner, not about renouncing possessions

tags.when_helps: Someone who thinks giving up possessions alone will free them from attachment.

display_text: The man who gives up living in houses, wearing fine clothes, and eating good food, and goes into the desert, may be a most attached person. A man may be on a throne and perfectly non-attached; another man may be in rags and still very much attached.
plain: Someone who gives up home and comforts for the desert can still be deeply attached, even to his body. Non-attachment is in the mind: one person on a throne can be free, another in rags bound.
core_idea: Non-attachment is in the mind, not outward circumstances.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: Look at those poor slaves to duty! Duty leaves them no time to say prayers, no time to bathe. Duty is ever on them. They go out and work. Duty is on them! They come home and think of the work for the next day. Duty is on them! It is living a slave’s life, at last dropping down in the street and dying in harness, like a horse.
note: Overwork and burnout; enslaved by obligation

tags.when_helps: A reader so ground down by duty they have no time for themselves.

display_text: Look at those poor slaves to duty! Duty leaves them no time to say prayers, no time to bathe. Duty is ever on them. They go out and work. Duty is on them! They come home and think of the work for the next day. Duty is on them! It is living a slave’s life, at last dropping down in the street and dying in harness, like a horse.
plain: Look at people enslaved by duty: no time to pray or bathe, working all day and planning tomorrow's work at night. It is a slave's life, ending in dropping dead in harness like a horse.
core_idea: Being enslaved by duty is a slave's life.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: Whatever you have to give to the world, do give by all means, but not as a duty. Do not take any thought of that. Be not compelled. Why should you be compelled? Everything that you do under compulsion goes to build up attachment.
note: Giving freely rather than from obligation

situations: caring for a sick or ageing relative
tags.when_helps: Someone giving out of compulsion who wants to give freely instead.

display_text: Whatever you have to give to the world, do give by all means, but not as a duty. Do not take any thought of that. Be not compelled. Why should you be compelled? Everything that you do under compulsion goes to build up attachment.
plain: Give whatever you have to give the world, but not out of duty or compulsion. Don't dwell on it. Everything done under compulsion builds attachment.
core_idea: Give freely, not from compulsion.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: Seek no praise, no reward, for anything you do. No sooner do we perform a good action than we begin to desire credit for it. No sooner do we give money to some charity than we want to see our names blazoned in the papers. Misery must come as the result of such desires. The greatest men in the world have passed away unknown.
note: Wanting recognition and credit for good deeds

tags.when_helps: A reader who wants recognition for the good they do.

display_text: Seek no praise, no reward, for anything you do. No sooner do we perform a good action than we begin to desire credit for it. No sooner do we give money to some charity than we want to see our names blazoned in the papers. Misery must come as the result of such desires. The greatest men in the world have passed away unknown.
plain: Seek no praise or reward for anything. The moment we do good we want credit; give to charity and we want our names in the papers. Such desires bring misery. The greatest people died unknown.
core_idea: Seek no credit; the greatest died unknown.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: The highest men are calm, silent, and unknown. They are the men who really know the power of thought; they are sure that, even if they go into a cave and close the door and simply think five true thoughts and then pass away, these five thoughts of theirs will live through eternity. Indeed such thoughts will penetrate through the mountains, cross the oceans, and travel through the world. They will enter deep into human hearts and brains and raise up men and women who will give them practical expression in the workings of human life.
note: Feeling unseen; quiet influence of true thought

tags.when_helps: Someone quiet and unknown who wonders whether their inner life makes any difference.

display_text: The highest men are calm, silent, and unknown. They are the men who really know the power of thought; they are sure that, even if they go into a cave and close the door and simply think five true thoughts and then pass away, these five thoughts of theirs will live through eternity. Indeed such thoughts will penetrate through the mountains, cross the oceans, and travel through the world. They will enter deep into human hearts and brains and raise up men and women who will give them practical expression in the workings of human life.
plain: The highest people are calm, quiet and unknown. They know the power of thought: even five true thoughts thought alone in a cave will live forever, travel the world, enter human hearts and inspire people to live them out.
core_idea: True thoughts, even unspoken, outlive us and spread.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VII. Freedom
text: Millions like you and me think that we are great people in the world; but we all die, and in five minutes the world forgets us.
note: Self-importance and mortality; humility

tags.when_helps: A reader taking their own importance too seriously.

display_text: Millions like you and me think that we are great people in the world; but we all die, and in five minutes the world forgets us.
plain: Millions of us think we are important in the world, but we all die, and within five minutes the world forgets us.
core_idea: The world quickly forgets us all.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VIII. The Ideal Of Karma-Yoga
text: The lamp is constantly burning out, and that is its life. If you want to have life, you have to die every moment for it. Life and death are only different expressions of the same thing looked at from different standpoints; they are the falling and the rising of the same wave, and the two form one whole. One looks at the “fall” side and becomes a pessimist another looks at the “rise” side and becomes an optimist.
note: Life and death as one; pessimism and optimism

tags.when_helps: Someone troubled by death who could see life and death as one movement.

display_text: The lamp is constantly burning out, and that is its life. If you want to have life, you have to die every moment for it. Life and death are only different expressions of the same thing looked at from different standpoints; they are the falling and the rising of the same wave, and the two form one whole. One looks at the “fall” side and becomes a pessimist; another looks at the “rise” side and becomes an optimist.
plain: A lamp lives by constantly burning out; to live, you must die every moment. Life and death are the falling and rising of one wave. The pessimist looks only at the fall, the optimist only at the rise.
core_idea: Life and death are one wave rising and falling.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VIII. The Ideal Of Karma-Yoga
text: When a boy is going to school and his father and mother are taking care of him, everything seems blessed to him; his wants are simple, he is a great optimist. But the old man, with his varied experience, becomes calmer and is sure to have his warmth considerably cooled down.
note: Ageing and losing youthful optimism

tags.when_helps: An older reader noticing their youthful optimism has cooled.

display_text: When a boy is going to school and his father and mother are taking care of him, everything seems blessed to him; his wants are simple, he is a great optimist. But the old man, with his varied experience, becomes calmer and is sure to have his warmth considerably cooled down.
plain: A schoolboy cared for by his parents finds everything wonderful; his needs are simple and he is full of optimism. An old man, after much experience, grows calmer and his warmth cools a great deal.
core_idea: Youth is hopeful; experience cools our enthusiasm.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VIII. The Ideal Of Karma-Yoga
text: This world’s wheel within wheel is a terrible mechanism; if we put our hands in it, as soon as we are caught we are gone. We all think that when we have done a certain duty, we shall be at rest; but before we have done a part of that duty, another is already in waiting. We are all being dragged along by this mighty, complex world-machine.
note: Endless obligations; never reaching rest

tags.when_helps: Someone who never reaches rest because another duty always waits.

display_text: This world’s wheel within wheel is a terrible mechanism; if we put our hands in it, as soon as we are caught we are gone. We all think that when we have done a certain duty, we shall be at rest; but before we have done a part of that duty, another is already in waiting. We are all being dragged along by this mighty, complex world-machine.
plain: The world is a terrible machine of wheels within wheels; once caught in it, we are lost. We think we will rest after finishing one duty, but another is already waiting. We are all dragged along by it.
core_idea: The world's demands never let us rest.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VIII. The Ideal Of Karma-Yoga
text: Let us do good because it is good to do good; he who does good work even in order to get to heaven binds himself down, says the Karma-Yogi. Any work that is done with any the least selfish motive, instead of making us free, forges one more chain for our feet.
note: Doing good without ulterior motive

tags.when_helps: A reader doing good with an eye on reward, even a spiritual one.

display_text: Let us do good because it is good to do good; he who does good work even in order to get to heaven binds himself down, says the Karma-Yogi. Any work that is done with any the least selfish motive, instead of making us free, forges one more chain for our feet.
plain: Do good because doing good is good. Even doing good to reach heaven binds you. Any work done with the slightest selfish motive adds another chain instead of freeing you.
core_idea: Do good for its own sake, or it binds you.

plain_judge.issue: Drops attribution to the Karma-Yogi, stating it as a direct claim.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VIII. The Ideal Of Karma-Yoga
text: Every good work we do without any ulterior motive, instead of forging a new chain, will break one of the links in the existing chains. Every good thought that we send to the world without thinking of any return, will be stored up there and break one link in the chain, and make us purer and purer, until we become the purest of mortals.
note: Small selfless acts gradually freeing us

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to become better who could start with simple acts of selfless good.

display_text: Every good work we do without any ulterior motive, instead of forging a new chain, will break one of the links in the existing chains. Every good thought that we send to the world without thinking of any return, will be stored up there and break one link in the chain, and make us purer and purer, until we become the purest of mortals.
plain: Every good act done without ulterior motive breaks a link in the chains that bind us. Every good thought sent out without expecting return breaks another, making us purer until we are purest of all.
core_idea: Selfless good deeds break our chains.

display: Karma-Yoga: Chapter VIII. The Ideal Of Karma-Yoga
text: He works best who works without any motive, neither for money, nor for fame, nor for anything else; and when a man can do that, he will be a Buddha, and out of him will come the power to work in such a manner as will transform the world.
note: Work without seeking money or fame

tags.when_helps: A worker driven by money or fame who wants a freer reason to work.

display_text: He works best who works without any motive, neither for money, nor for fame, nor for anything else; and when a man can do that, he will be a Buddha, and out of him will come the power to work in such a manner as will transform the world.
plain: The best worker works with no motive at all, not for money, fame or anything else. Whoever can do that becomes a Buddha, and from him comes the power to work in a way that transforms the world.
core_idea: Working without motive transforms the world.

display: Raja-Yoga: Preface
text: Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this Divinity within by controlling nature, external and internal. Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy — by one, or more, or all of these — and be free. This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details.
note: Spiritual seeking beyond dogma; inner divinity

tags.when_helps: Someone put off by religious dogma who wants a simpler view of spiritual life.

display_text: Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this Divinity within by controlling nature, external and internal. Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy — by one, or more, or all of these — and be free. This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details.
plain: Every soul is divine at heart; the goal is to bring out that divinity by mastering nature outside and within, through work, worship, mind control or philosophy, and be free. Doctrines, rituals and temples are secondary.
core_idea: Religion is manifesting the divinity within the soul.

plain_judge.issue: 'Potentially divine' becomes 'divine at heart'; drops 'this is the whole of religion'.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter I. Introductory
text: What right has a man to say he has a soul if he does not feel it, or that there is a God if he does not see Him? If there is a God we must see Him, if there is a soul we must perceive it; otherwise it is better not to believe. It is better to be an outspoken atheist than a hypocrite.
note: Religious doubt; honesty over borrowed belief

tags.when_helps: A doubter who values honesty and won't pretend to believe what they haven't experienced.

display_text: What right has a man to say he has a soul if he does not feel it, or that there is a God if he does not see Him? If there is a God we must see Him, if there is a soul we must perceive it; otherwise it is better not to believe. It is better to be an outspoken atheist than a hypocrite.
plain: What right has anyone to claim a soul or God without feeling or seeing them? If they exist we must experience them; otherwise better not to believe. An honest atheist is better than a hypocrite.
core_idea: An honest atheist beats a hypocritical believer.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter I. Introductory
text: When by analysing his own mind, man comes face to face, as it were, with something which is never destroyed, something which is, by its own nature, eternally pure and perfect, he will no more be miserable, no more unhappy. All misery comes from fear, from unsatisfied desire. Man will find that he never dies, and then he will have no more fear of death. When he knows that he is perfect, he will have no more vain desires, and both these causes being absent, there will be no more misery — there will be perfect bliss, even while in this body.
note: Fear and unsatisfied desire as roots of misery

tags.when_helps: Someone whose unhappiness comes from fear and wanting who seeks a deeper source of peace.

display_text: When by analysing his own mind, man comes face to face, as it were, with something which is never destroyed, something which is, by its own nature, eternally pure and perfect, he will no more be miserable, no more unhappy. All misery comes from fear, from unsatisfied desire. Man will find that he never dies, and then he will have no more fear of death. When he knows that he is perfect, he will have no more vain desires, and both these causes being absent, there will be no more misery — there will be perfect bliss, even while in this body.
plain: Looking deep into his mind, a person can find something eternally pure and perfect. Misery comes from fear and unmet desire; knowing he never dies and is already perfect, he loses both and finds bliss.
core_idea: Knowing your undying, perfect nature ends misery.

plain_judge.issue: Drops 'even while in this body'.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter I. Introductory
text: The world is ready to give up its secrets if we only know how to knock, how to give it the necessary blow. The strength and force of the blow come through concentration. There is no limit to the power of the human mind. The more concentrated it is, the more power is brought to bear on one point; that is the secret.
note: Focus and concentration; the mind's power

tags.when_helps: A reader whose scattered mind is keeping them from solving a problem.

display_text: The world is ready to give up its secrets if we only know how to knock, how to give it the necessary blow. The strength and force of the blow come through concentration. There is no limit to the power of the human mind. The more concentrated it is, the more power is brought to bear on one point; that is the secret.
plain: The world will give up its secrets if we knock hard enough, and that force comes from concentration. The mind's power has no limit; the more it focuses on one point, the more power it has.
core_idea: Concentration is the secret of the mind's power.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter I. Introductory
text: We are human beings; that is sufficient. Every human being has the right and the power to seek for religion. Every human being has the right to ask the reason, why, and to have his question answered by himself, if he only takes the trouble.
note: Seeking meaning; right to question for oneself

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels unqualified to question or explore religion for themselves.

display_text: We are human beings; that is sufficient. Every human being has the right and the power to seek for religion. Every human being has the right to ask the reason, why, and to have his question answered by himself, if he only takes the trouble.
plain: Being human is enough. Every person has the right and the power to seek religion, to ask why, and to find the answer for themselves if they take the trouble.
core_idea: Everyone has the right to seek truth themselves.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter I. Introductory
text: If the body is sick, the mind becomes sick also. If the body is healthy, the mind remains healthy and strong. When one is angry, the mind becomes disturbed. Similarly when the mind is disturbed, the body also becomes disturbed.
note: Body and mind affecting each other

tags.when_helps: A reader noticing how illness or anger in one of body or mind upsets the other.

display_text: If the body is sick, the mind becomes sick also. If the body is healthy, the mind remains healthy and strong. When one is angry, the mind becomes disturbed. Similarly when the mind is disturbed, the body also becomes disturbed.
plain: When the body is sick the mind gets sick too, and when the body is healthy the mind stays strong. Anger disturbs the mind, and a disturbed mind disturbs the body.
core_idea: Body and mind affect each other.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter I. Introductory
text: The best guide in life is strength. In religion, as in all other matters, discard everything that weakens you, have nothing to do with it.
note: Choosing what strengthens rather than weakens you

tags.when_helps: Someone weighed down by beliefs or habits that drain their strength.

display_text: The best guide in life is strength. In religion, as in all other matters, discard everything that weakens you, have nothing to do with it.
plain: Strength is the best guide in life. In religion as in everything, reject whatever makes you weak and have nothing to do with it.
core_idea: Reject whatever makes you weak.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter I. Introductory
text: While the plant is growing it must be hedged round, lest it be injured; but when it becomes a tree, the hedges are taken away. It is strong enough to withstand all assaults.
note: Protecting oneself while growing; vulnerability early on

tags.when_helps: Someone early in a change who needs to protect themselves until they are stronger.

display_text: While the plant is growing it must be hedged round, lest it be injured; but when it becomes a tree, the hedges are taken away. It is strong enough to withstand all assaults.
plain: A young plant needs a fence around it so it isn't damaged; once it becomes a tree, the fence is removed, because it can withstand anything.
core_idea: Protect what is young until it grows strong.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. The First Steps
text: Practice is absolutely necessary. You may sit down and listen to me by the hour every day, but if you do not practice, you will not get one step further. It all depends on practice. We never understand these things until we experience them. We will have to see and feel them for ourselves. Simply listening to explanations and theories will not do.
note: Learning through practice, not theory

tags.when_helps: A reader who reads and listens a lot but hasn't yet begun to practise.

display_text: Practice is absolutely necessary. You may sit down and listen to me by the hour every day, but if you do not practice, you will not get one step further. It all depends on practice. We never understand these things until we experience them. We will have to see and feel them for ourselves. Simply listening to explanations and theories will not do.
plain: Practice is essential. You can listen to me for hours every day, but without practice you won't move a step. We only understand these things by experiencing and feeling them ourselves; theories are not enough.
core_idea: Only practice and experience bring understanding.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. The First Steps
text: No man was ever born who could stop his body one moment from changing. Body is the name of a series of changes. “As in a river the masses of water are changing before you every moment, and new masses are coming, yet taking similar form, so is it with this body.” Yet the body must be kept strong and healthy. It is the best instrument we have.
note: Ageing body; constant change; caring for health

tags.when_helps: Someone uneasy about their changing body who still wants to keep it healthy.

display_text: No man was ever born who could stop his body one moment from changing. Body is the name of a series of changes. “As in a river the masses of water are changing before you every moment, and new masses are coming, yet taking similar form, so is it with this body.” Yet the body must be kept strong and healthy. It is the best instrument we have.
plain: No one can stop the body changing even for a moment; it is a flow, like a river whose water is always new yet looks the same. Still, keep it strong and healthy: it is our best instrument.
core_idea: The ever-changing body is still our best instrument.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. The First Steps
text: Sit in a straight posture, and the first thing to do is to send a current of holy thought to all creation. Mentally repeat, “Let all beings be happy; let all beings be peaceful; let all beings be blissful.” So do to the east, south, north and west. The more you do that the better you will feel yourself. You will find at last that the easiest way to make ourselves healthy is to see that others are healthy, and the easiest way to make ourselves happy is to see that others are happy.
note: Meditation of goodwill; happiness through wishing others well

tags.when_helps: A reader wanting a simple practice of goodwill that also lifts their own spirits.

display_text: Sit in a straight posture, and the first thing to do is to send a current of holy thought to all creation. Mentally repeat, “Let all beings be happy; let all beings be peaceful; let all beings be blissful.” So do to the east, south, north and west. The more you do that the better you will feel yourself. You will find at last that the easiest way to make ourselves healthy is to see that others are healthy, and the easiest way to make ourselves happy is to see that others are happy.
plain: Sit upright and silently wish all beings, in every direction, to be happy, peaceful and blissful. The more you do it, the better you feel; making others happy and healthy is the easiest way to be so yourself.
core_idea: Wishing others happiness makes us happy.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. The First Steps
text: Freedom is never to be reached by the weak. Throw away all weakness. Tell your body that it is strong, tell your mind that it is strong, and have unbounded faith and hope in yourself.
note: Self-doubt and weakness; believing in yourself

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling weak who needs encouragement to believe in their own strength.

display_text: Freedom is never to be reached by the weak. Throw away all weakness. Tell your body that it is strong, tell your mind that it is strong, and have unbounded faith and hope in yourself.
plain: The weak never reach freedom. Throw off all weakness: tell your body and your mind that they are strong, and have boundless faith and hope in yourself.
core_idea: Throw off weakness and believe in yourself.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter III. Prana
text: Each man must begin where he stands, must learn how to control the things that are nearest to him. This body is very near to us, nearer than anything in the external universe, and this mind is the nearest of all.
note: Feeling overwhelmed; starting with what is closest

tags.when_helps: A reader overwhelmed by everything they can't control, unsure where to begin.

display_text: Each man must begin where he stands, must learn how to control the things that are nearest to him. This body is very near to us, nearer than anything in the external universe, and this mind is the nearest of all.
plain: Everyone has to start where they are and learn to control what is closest to them. The body is closer than anything in the outside world, and the mind is closest of all.
core_idea: Begin by mastering what is nearest: body and mind.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter III. Prana
text: Everything is infectious in this world, good or bad. If your body be in a certain state of tension, it will have a tendency to produce the same tension in others. If you are strong and healthy, those that live near you will also have the tendency to become strong and healthy, but if you are sick and weak, those around you will have the tendency to become the same.
note: How our state affects the people around us

situations: caring for a sick or ageing relative
tags.when_helps: Someone noticing how their tension spreads to those around them.

display_text: Everything is infectious in this world, good or bad. If your body be in a certain state of tension, it will have a tendency to produce the same tension in others. If you are strong and healthy, those that live near you will also have the tendency to become strong and healthy, but if you are sick and weak, those around you will have the tendency to become the same.
plain: Everything in this world is catching, good or bad. If you are tense, strong or sick, those near you tend to become the same.
core_idea: Strength and weakness are both contagious.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter III. Prana
text: In an ocean there are huge waves, like mountains, then smaller waves, and still smaller, down to little bubbles, but back of all these is the infinite ocean. The bubble is connected with the infinite ocean at one end, and the huge wave at the other end. So, one may be a gigantic man, and another a little bubble, but each is connected with that infinite ocean of energy, which is the common birthright of every animal that exists. Wherever there is life, the storehouse of infinite energy is behind it.
note: Feeling small or insignificant compared to others

tags.when_helps: A reader who feels small and insignificant beside others.

display_text: In an ocean there are huge waves, like mountains, then smaller waves, and still smaller, down to little bubbles, but back of all these is the infinite ocean. The bubble is connected with the infinite ocean at one end, and the huge wave at the other end. So, one may be a gigantic man, and another a little bubble, but each is connected with that infinite ocean of energy, which is the common birthright of every animal that exists. Wherever there is life, the storehouse of infinite energy is behind it.
plain: The ocean has mountainous waves, small waves and tiny bubbles, but behind them all is the infinite ocean. Likewise, great or small, every living being is connected to the same infinite store of energy behind all life.
core_idea: Every life draws on the same infinite energy.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter V. The Control Of Psychic Prana
text: The first lesson is just to breathe in a measured way, in and out. That will harmonise the system. When you have practiced this for some time, you will do well to join to it the repetition of some word as “Om,” or any other sacred word. In India we use certain symbolical words instead of counting one, two, three, four. That is why I advise you to join the mental repetition of the “Om,” or some other sacred word to the Pranayama. Let the word flow in and out with the breath, rhythmically, harmoniously, and you will find the whole body is becoming rhythmical. Then you will learn what rest is. Compared with it, sleep is not rest. Once this rest comes the most tired nerves will be calmed down, and you will find that you have never before really rested.
note: Exhaustion and finding real rest through calm breathing

tags.when_helps: Someone with tired, frayed nerves who wants a simple breathing practice for real rest.

text: We hear “Be good,” and “Be good,” and “Be good,” taught all over the world. There is hardly a child, born in any country in the world, who has not been told, “Do not steal,” “Do not tell a lie,” but nobody tells the child how he can help doing them. Talking will not help him. Why should he not become a thief? We do not teach him how not to steal; we simply tell him, “Do not steal.” Only when we teach him to control his mind do we really help him.
note: Teaching children self-control rather than just rules

tags.when_helps: A parent frustrated that telling a child to be good isn't working.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter VI. Pratyahara And Dharana
text: How hard it is to control the mind! Well has it been compared to the maddened monkey. There was a monkey, restless by his own nature, as all monkeys are. As if that were not enough some one made him drink freely of wine, so that he became still more restless. Then a scorpion stung him. When a man is stung by a scorpion, he jumps about for a whole day; so the poor monkey found his condition worse than ever. To complete his misery a demon entered into him. What language can describe the uncontrollable restlessness of that monkey? The human mind is like that monkey, incessantly active by its own nature; then it becomes drunk with the wine of desire, thus increasing its turbulence. After desire takes possession comes the sting of the scorpion of jealousy at the success of others, and last of all the demon of pride enters the mind, making it think itself of all importance. How hard to control such a mind!
note: Restless mind driven by desire, jealousy and pride

tags.when_helps: Someone struggling with a restless, jumpy mind, reassured that this is universal.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter VI. Pratyahara And Dharana
text: Knowledge is power, says the proverb, and that is true. Until you know what the mind is doing you cannot control it. Give it the rein; many hideous thoughts may come into it; you will be astonished that it was possible for you to think such thoughts. But you will find that each day the mind’s vagaries are becoming less and less violent, that each day it is becoming calmer. In the first few months you will find that the mind will have a great many thoughts, later you will find that they have somewhat decreased, and in a few more months they will be fewer and fewer, until at last the mind will be under perfect control; but we must patiently practice every day.
note: Disturbing thoughts in meditation; patience as the mind calms

tags.when_helps: A meditator alarmed by unwanted thoughts, reassured they settle with patient practice.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter VI. Pratyahara And Dharana
text: Be like the pearl oyster. There is a pretty Indian fable to the effect that if it rains when the star Svâti is in the ascendant, and a drop of rain falls into an oyster, that drop becomes a pearl. The oysters know this, so they come to the surface when that star shines, and wait to catch the precious raindrop. When a drop falls into them, quickly the oysters close their shells and dive down to the bottom of the sea, there to patiently develop the drop into the pearl. We should be like that. First hear, then understand, and then, leaving all distractions, shut your minds to outside influences, and devote yourselves to developing the truth within you.
note: Patiently nurturing what you have learned, away from distraction

tags.when_helps: Someone distracted by too many influences who wants to focus and let an idea grow.

text: There is the danger of frittering away your energies by taking up an idea only for its novelty, and then giving it up for another that is newer. Take one thing up and do it, and see the end of it, and before you have seen the end, do not give it up. He who can become mad with an idea, he alone sees light. Those that only take a nibble here and a nibble there will never attain anything.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter VII. Dhyana And Samadhi
text: Experience is the only teacher we have. We may talk and reason all our lives, but we shall not understand a word of truth, until we experience it ourselves. You cannot hope to make a man a surgeon by simply giving him a few books. You cannot satisfy my curiosity to see a country by showing me a map; I must have actual experience. Maps can only create curiosity in us to get more perfect knowledge. Beyond that, they have no value whatever.
note: Learning through lived experience, not just reading or talk

tags.when_helps: A reader tired of theory who needs to learn by doing.

text: So long as there is desire, no real happiness can come. It is only the contemplative, witness-like study of objects that brings to us real enjoyment and happiness. The animal has its happiness in the senses, the man in his intellect, and the god in spiritual contemplation. It is only to the soul that has attained to this contemplative state that the world really becomes beautiful. To him who desires nothing, and does not mix himself up with them, the manifold changes of nature are one panorama of beauty and sublimity.
note: Restless wanting versus contentment and seeing beauty

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Raja-Yoga In Brief
text: “He who hates none, who is the friend of all, who is merciful to all, who has nothing of his own, who is free from egoism, who is even-minded in pain and pleasure, who is forbearing, who is always satisfied, who works always in Yoga, whose self has become controlled, whose will is firm, whose mind and intellect are given up unto Me, such a one is My beloved Bhakta. text: It is the greatest manifestation of power to be calm. It is easy to be active. Let the reins go, and the horses will run away with you. You must not mistake Sattva for dullness or laziness. The calm man is the one who has control over the mind waves. Activity is the manifestation of inferior strength, calmness, of the superior.

text: The only remedy for bad habits is counter habits; all the bad habits that have left their impressions are to be controlled by good habits. Never say any man is hopeless, because he only represents a character, a bundle of habits, which can be checked by new and better ones. Character is repeated habits, and repeated habits alone can reform character.

text: The ignorant man thinks his body is the Soul. The learned man thinks his mind is the Soul. But both of them are mistaken. What makes the Soul get mingled up with all this? If it is one of love, we see ourselves reflected in that wave, and say we are loving. If that wave is one of weakness, and the Soul is reflected in it, we think we are weak.

text: The organs are the horses, the mind is the rein, the intellect is the charioteer, the soul is the rider, and the body is the chariot. But if the organs, the horses, are well controlled, and if the rein, the mind, is well held in the hands of the charioteer, the intellect, the chariot reaches the goal.

text: “Surrendering the fruits of work to God” is to take to ourselves neither credit nor blame, but to give up both to the Lord and be at peace.
note: Letting go of praise and blame for one's work

plain: Surrendering the results of work to God means taking neither credit nor blame for yourself, giving both to the Lord, and being at peace.
core_idea: Give credit and blame to God and be at peace.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: When I am angry, my whole mind becomes a huge wave of anger. I feel it, see it, handle it, can easily manipulate it, can fight with it; but I shall not succeed perfectly in the fight until I can get down below to its causes. A man says something very harsh to me, and I begin to feel that I am getting heated, and he goes on till I am perfectly angry and forget myself, identify myself with anger. When he first began to abuse me, I thought, “I am going to be angry”. Anger was one thing, and I was another; but when I became angry, I was anger. These feelings have to be controlled in the germ, the root, in their fine forms, before even we have become conscious that they are acting on us.
note: Being swept away by anger when insulted

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone who gets swept away by anger when provoked and wants to catch it earlier.

display_text: When I am angry, my whole mind becomes a huge wave of anger. core_idea: Control anger at its root, before it takes over.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: All happiness which comes from the senses will, eventually, bring pain. All enjoyment will make us thirst for more, and that brings pain as its result. There is no limit to man’s desires; he goes on desiring, and when he comes to a point where desire cannot be fulfilled, the result is pain.
note: Endless desire, craving, dissatisfaction

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: A reader chasing pleasure and finding it always leaves them wanting.

display_text: All happiness which comes from the senses will, eventually, bring pain. All enjoyment will make us thirst for more, and that brings pain as its result. There is no limit to man’s desires; he goes on desiring, and when he comes to a point where desire cannot be fulfilled, the result is pain.
plain: All happiness from the senses eventually brings pain. Every pleasure makes us want more, and human desire has no limit; when desire can't be satisfied, pain follows.
core_idea: Sense pleasures breed endless desire and pain.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: The great king Yudhishthira once said that the most wonderful thing in life is that every moment we see people dying around us, and yet we think we shall never die. Surrounded by fools on every side, we think we are the only exceptions, the only learned men. Surrounded by all sorts of experiences of fickleness, we think our love is the only lasting love.
note: Denial of mortality and impermanence

tags.when_helps: Someone living as though they are the exception to death and change.

display_text: The great king Yudhishthira once said that the most wonderful thing in life is that every moment we see people dying around us, and yet we think we shall never die. Surrounded by fools on every side, we think we are the only exceptions, the only learned men. Surrounded by all sorts of experiences of fickleness, we think our love is the only lasting love.
plain: King Yudhishthira said the greatest wonder is that we see people dying every moment yet think we will never die. Amid fools we think ourselves wise; amid fickleness we think our love alone will last.
core_idea: We see death everywhere yet think we won't die.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: Experience is the one great teacher — experience of pleasure and pain — but know it is only experience.
note: Learning from both good and painful times

tags.when_helps: A reader caught up in pleasure or pain who could see it as a passing teacher.

display_text: Experience is the one great teacher — experience of pleasure and pain — but know it is only experience.
plain: Experience of pleasure and pain is the one great teacher, but remember that it is only experience.
core_idea: Experience teaches, but it is only experience.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: It is not the building, but the people that make a church, and that is what we always forget.
note: Community and people matter more than places

tags.when_helps: Someone disillusioned with religious institutions who values the community itself.

display_text: It is not the building, but the people that make a church, and that is what we always forget.
plain: It is the people, not the building, that make a church, and we always forget that.
core_idea: People, not buildings, make a church.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: Two facts come into our consciousness, and stand or fall with each other. These are our notions of bondage and freedom. If we want to go through a wall, and our head bumps against that wall, we see we are limited by that wall. At the same time we find a willpower, and think we can direct our will everywhere. At every step these contradictory ideas come to us. We have to believe that we are free, yet at every moment we find we are not free.
note: Feeling both free and trapped; limits and will

tags.when_helps: A reader feeling both free and hemmed in, puzzling over the limits on their will.

display_text: Two facts come into our consciousness, and stand or fall with each other. These are our notions of bondage and freedom. If we want to go through a wall, and our head bumps against that wall, we see we are limited by that wall. At the same time we find a willpower, and think we can direct our will everywhere. plain: Two opposite ideas come together: that we are bound and that we are free. A wall shows our limits, yet our will feels boundless. We must believe we are free, yet at every moment find we are not.
core_idea: We feel both bound and free at once.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal. Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy — by one or more or all of these — and be free. This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details.
note: Purpose; inner potential; many paths to the same goal

tags.when_helps: Someone tired of rituals and doctrines who wants the heart of spiritual life.

display_text: Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal. Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy — by one or more or all of these — and be free. This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: While we are aware of thirsting after knowledge, we begin to seek here and there, wherever we think we can get some truth, and failing to find it we become dissatisfied and seek in a fresh direction. All search is vain, until we begin to perceive that knowledge is within ourselves, that no one can help us, that we must help ourselves.
note: Restless searching for answers; self-reliance

tags.when_helps: A seeker who keeps looking elsewhere for answers and keeps coming away dissatisfied.

display_text: While we are aware of thirsting after knowledge, we begin to seek here and there, wherever we think we can get some truth, and failing to find it we become dissatisfied and seek in a fresh direction. All search is vain, until we begin to perceive that knowledge is within ourselves, that no one can help us, that we must help ourselves.
plain: Hungry for knowledge, we search everywhere, and failing, grow dissatisfied and look elsewhere. All searching is useless until we see that knowledge is within us, that no one else can help us, and that we must help ourselves.
core_idea: Knowledge is within; we must help ourselves.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: For instance, when a big wave of anger has come into the mind, how are we to control that? Just by raising an opposing wave. Think of love. Sometimes a mother is very angry with her husband, and while in that state, the baby comes in, and she kisses the baby; the old wave dies out and a new wave arises, love for the child. That suppresses the other one. Love is opposite to anger.
note: Calming anger by turning toward love

tags.when_helps: Someone in the grip of anger at a partner or family member who needs a way to turn it.

display_text: For instance, when a big wave of anger has come into the mind, how are we to control that? Just by raising an opposing wave. Think of love. Sometimes a mother is very angry with her husband, and while in that state, the baby comes in, and she kisses the baby; the old wave dies out and a new wave arises, love for the child. That suppresses the other one. Love is opposite to anger.
plain: To control a big wave of anger, raise an opposite wave: think of love. An angry mother who kisses her baby finds the anger fading as love for the child rises. Love is the opposite of anger.
core_idea: Counter anger by raising love.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: Every vicious thought will rebound, every thought of hatred which you may have thought, in a cave even, is stored up, and will one day come back to you with tremendous power in the form of some misery here. If you project hatred and jealousy, they will rebound on you with compound interest. No power can avert them; when once you have put them in motion, you will have to bear them.
note: Hatred and jealousy harm the one who holds them

tags.when_helps: A reader nursing hatred or jealousy, warned that it rebounds on them.

display_text: Every vicious thought will rebound, every thought of hatred which you may have thought, in a cave even, is stored up, and will one day come back to you with tremendous power in the form of some misery here. If you project hatred and jealousy, they will rebound on you with compound interest. No power can avert them; when once you have put them in motion, you will have to bear them.
plain: Every hateful thought, even one thought alone in a cave, is stored up and will return to you as misery. Hatred and jealousy come back with compound interest; once set in motion, you must bear them.
core_idea: Hateful thoughts return to us with interest.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter II. Concentration: Its Practice
text: The first sign that you are becoming religious is that you are becoming cheerful. When a man is gloomy, that may be dyspepsia, but it is not religion.

display_text: The first sign that you are becoming religious is that you are becoming cheerful. When a man is gloomy, that may be dyspepsia, but it is not religion.
plain: The first sign you are becoming religious is that you are becoming cheerful. Gloominess may be indigestion, but it is not religion.
core_idea: Cheerfulness is the first sign of real religion.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter III. Powers
text: The more time passes unnoticed the more concentrated we are. In common life we see that when we are interested in a book we do not note the time at all, and when we leave the book, we are often surprised to find how many hours have passed.

tags.when_helps: A reader who notices how deep absorption makes time vanish and wants more of it.

display_text: The more time passes unnoticed the more concentrated we are. In common life we see that when we are interested in a book we do not note the time at all, and when we leave the book, we are often surprised to find how many hours have passed.
plain: The more time slips by unnoticed, the more concentrated we are. Absorbed in a book, we lose track of time and are surprised how many hours have passed.
core_idea: Losing track of time shows deep concentration.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter III. Powers
text: The misery that we suffer comes from ignorance, from non-discrimination between the real and the unreal. We all take the bad for the good, the dream for the reality. Soul is the only reality, and we have forgotten it.
note: Source of suffering; confusing the unreal for the real

tags.when_helps: Someone caught in recurring misery who is open to seeing it as forgetting their deeper, real self.

display_text: The misery that we suffer comes from ignorance, from non-discrimination between the real and the unreal. We all take the bad for the good, the dream for the reality. Soul is the only reality, and we have forgotten it.
plain: Our misery comes from ignorance, from failing to tell the real from the unreal. We mistake bad for good and the dream for reality. The Soul is the only reality, and we have forgotten it.
core_idea: Misery comes from forgetting the Soul, the only reality.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter IV. Independence
text: We are living in the midst of such a mass of miracles, day and night, that we do not think anything of them.
note: Taking everyday wonders for granted; gratitude

tags.when_helps: Someone whose days feel flat and routine, ready to notice the wonder they have stopped seeing.

display_text: We are living in the midst of such a mass of miracles, day and night, that we do not think anything of them.
plain: We live surrounded by so many miracles, day and night, that we think nothing of them.
core_idea: We ignore the miracles all around us.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter IV. Independence
text: The water for irrigation of fields is already in the canal, only shut in by gates. The farmer opens these gates, and the water flows in by itself, by the law of gravitation. So all progress and power are already in every man; perfection is man’s nature, only it is barred in and prevented from taking its proper course. If anyone can take the bar off, in rushes nature.
note: Self-doubt; potential already within, only blocked

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels blocked or inadequate and needs to hear their potential is already within, waiting to be released.

display_text: The water for irrigation of fields is already in the canal, only shut in by gates. The farmer opens these gates, and the water flows in by itself, by the law of gravitation. plain: Irrigation water waits in the canal behind gates; open them and it flows in by itself. Likewise all progress and power are already in everyone; perfection is our nature, and once the barrier is removed it rushes in.
core_idea: Perfection is already within; remove the barrier.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter IV. Independence
text: Whatever you do never destroys your own glory, your own nature, because the soul cannot be acted upon by anything, only a veil is spread before it, hiding its perfection.
note: Guilt over past deeds; inner worth remains intact

display_text: Whatever you do never destroys your own glory, your own nature, because the soul cannot be acted upon by anything, only a veil is spread before it, hiding its perfection.
plain: Nothing you do can ever destroy your own glory or true nature, because nothing can touch the soul; a veil is only drawn over it, hiding its perfection.
core_idea: Nothing you do can destroy the soul's glory.

display: Raja-Yoga: Chapter IV. Independence
text: Nature’s task is done, this unselfish task which our sweet nurse, nature, had imposed upon herself. She gently took the self-forgetting soul by the hand, as it were, and showed him all the experiences in the universe, all manifestations, bringing him higher and higher through various bodies, till his lost glory came back, and he remembered his own nature. Then the kind mother went back the same way she came, for others who also have lost their way in the trackless desert of life. And thus is she working, without beginning and without end. And thus through pleasure and pain, through good and evil, the infinite river of souls is flowing into the ocean of perfection, of self-realisation.
note: Feeling lost; life's experiences leading us home

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling lost in life's pleasures and pains who wants a vast, hopeful view of where it all leads.

display_text: Nature’s task is done, this unselfish task which our sweet nurse, nature, had imposed upon herself. display: Raja-Yoga: Appendix
text: As the hawk becomes unhappy if the food is taken away from him and happy if he gives it up himself (so he who gives up everything voluntarily is happy).

display_text: As the hawk becomes unhappy if the food is taken away from him and happy if he gives it up himself (so he who gives up everything voluntarily is happy).
plain: A hawk is miserable if its food is taken away but happy if it gives the food up itself; so whoever gives everything up willingly is happy.
core_idea: Giving up willingly brings happiness.

display: Raja-Yoga: Appendix
text: Although devotion is to be given to many institutes and teachers, the essence is to be taken from them all as the bee takes the essence from many flowers.

display_text: Although devotion is to be given to many institutes and teachers, the essence is to be taken from them all as the bee takes the essence from many flowers.

core_idea: Take the essence from every teacher.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter I. The Necessity Of Religion
text: Every human being, whosoever and wheresoever he may be, has an ideal of infinite power. Every human being has an ideal of infinite pleasure. Most of the works that we find around us, the activities displayed everywhere, are due to the struggle for this infinite power or this infinite pleasure. But a few quickly discover that although they are struggling for infinite power, it is not through the senses that it can be reached. They find out very soon that that infinite pleasure is not to be got through the senses, or, in other words, the senses are too limited, and the body is too limited, to express the Infinite.
note: Restless striving; pleasure and power never satisfy

tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps chasing power or pleasure and senses it can never fully satisfy them.

display_text: Every human being, whosoever and wheresoever he may be, has an ideal of infinite power. Every human being has an ideal of infinite pleasure. plain: Everyone seeks infinite power and infinite pleasure, and most human activity is that struggle. A few soon discover these cannot be reached through the senses, because the senses and body are too limited to express the Infinite.
core_idea: The senses are too limited to reach the Infinite.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter I. The Necessity Of Religion
text: Ethics always says, “Not I, but thou.” Its motto is, “Not self, but non-self.” The vain ideas of individualism, to which man clings when he is trying to find that Infinite Power or that Infinite Pleasure through the senses, have to be given up — say the laws of ethics. You have to put yourself last, and others before you. The senses say, “Myself first.” Ethics says, “I must hold myself last.”
note: Selfishness versus putting others first

tags.when_helps: Someone wrestling with selfishness who wants a clear reminder to put others before themselves.

display_text: Ethics always says, “Not I, but thou.” Its motto is, “Not self, but non-self.” The vain ideas of individualism, to which man clings when he is trying to find that Infinite Power or that Infinite Pleasure through the senses, have to be given up — say the laws of ethics. You have to put yourself last, and others before you. The senses say, “Myself first.” Ethics says, “I must hold myself last.”
plain: Ethics says 'not I, but you'. It asks us to drop the vain individualism we cling to while seeking the Infinite through the senses. The senses say 'me first'; ethics says 'I must put myself last'.
core_idea: Ethics says: put yourself last.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter I. The Necessity Of Religion
text: It is good and very grand to conquer external nature, but grander still to conquer our internal nature. It is grand and good to know the laws that govern the stars and planets; it is infinitely grander and better to know the laws that govern the passions, the feelings, the will, of mankind.
note: Mastering one's own passions and feelings

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone struggling with their own passions or will who needs to see inner mastery as the greater achievement.

display_text: It is good and very grand to conquer external nature, but grander still to conquer our internal nature. It is grand and good to know the laws that govern the stars and planets; it is infinitely grander and better to know the laws that govern the passions, the feelings, the will, of mankind.
plain: Conquering outer nature is grand, but conquering our inner nature is grander. Knowing the laws of the stars and planets is good; knowing the laws of human passions, feelings and will is far better.
core_idea: Mastering inner nature is greater than outer.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: Yet, so long as there is death, the question must come again and again, “Is death the end of all these things to which we are clinging, as if they were the most real of all realities, the most substantial of all substances?” The world vanishes in a moment and is gone. Standing on the brink of a precipice beyond which is the infinite yawning chasm, every mind, however hardened, is bound to recoil and ask, “Is this real?” The hopes of a lifetime, built up little by little with all the energies of a great mind, vanish in a second. Are they real? This question must be answered. Time never lessens its power; on the other hand, it adds strength to it.
note: Facing death; questioning what is real and lasting

tags.when_helps: Someone shaken by death or sudden loss, asking whether anything they cling to is truly real.

display_text: Yet, so long as there is death, the question must come again and again, “Is death the end of all these things to which we are clinging, as if they were the most real of all realities, the most substantial of all substances?” The world vanishes in a moment and is gone. Standing on the brink of a precipice beyond which is the infinite yawning chasm, every mind, however hardened, is bound to recoil and ask, “Is this real?” The hopes of a lifetime, built up little by little with all the energies of a great mind, vanish in a second. core_idea: Death forces us to ask what is real.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: We run after everything to make ourselves happy; we pursue our mad career in the external world of senses. If you ask the young man with whom life is successful, he will declare that it is real; and he really thinks so. Perhaps, when the same man grows old and finds fortune ever eluding him, he will then declare that it is fate. He finds at last that his desires cannot be fulfilled. Wherever he goes, there is an adamantine wall beyond which he cannot pass. Every sense-activity results in a reaction. Everything is evanescent. Enjoyment, misery, luxury, wealth, power, and poverty, even life itself, are all evanescent.
note: Chasing happiness; ageing; everything passes

situations: loss of a dream or plan
tags.when_helps: Someone realising that success, wealth or pleasure have not delivered the lasting happiness they expected.

display_text: We run after everything to make ourselves happy; we pursue our mad career in the external world of senses. If you ask the young man with whom life is successful, he will declare that it is real; and he really thinks so. Perhaps, when the same man grows old and finds fortune ever eluding him, he will then declare that it is fate. He finds at last that his desires cannot be fulfilled.
