plain: We chase the senses to be happy. The successful young man calls life real; old and unfulfilled, he calls it fate, facing a wall he cannot pass. Pleasure, wealth, power, even life itself, all pass away.
core_idea: Everything we chase for happiness passes away.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: He alone lives whose life is in the whole universe, and the more we concentrate our lives on limited things, the faster we go towards death. Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living. When he can say, “I am in everything, in everybody, I am in all lives, I am the universe,” then alone comes the state of fearlessness.
note: Fear of death; living for others, not a small life

tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of death who might find courage in seeing their life as part of all life.

display_text: He alone lives whose life is in the whole universe, and the more we concentrate our lives on limited things, the faster we go towards death. Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living. plain: Only someone whose life is in the whole universe truly lives; narrowing life to small things brings death and its fear. That fear ends only when you can say: I am in everything, in all lives; I am the universe.
core_idea: Seeing yourself in all life ends fear of death.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: After long searches here and there, in temples and in churches, in earths and in heavens, at last you come back, completing the circle from where you started, to your own soul and find that He for whom you have been seeking all over the world, for whom you have been weeping and praying in churches and temples, on whom you were looking as the mystery of all mysteries shrouded in the clouds, is nearest of the near, is your own Self, the reality of your life, body, and soul. That is your own nature. Assert it, manifest it. Not to become pure, you are pure already. You are not to be perfect, you are that already.
note: Searching outside for what is already within

tags.when_helps: A spiritual seeker exhausted from searching everywhere, needing to hear that what they seek is already within.

display_text: After long searches here and there, in temples and in churches, in earths and in heavens, at last you come back, completing the circle from where you started, to your own soul and find that He for whom you have been seeking all over the world, for whom you have been weeping and praying in churches and temples, on whom you were looking as the mystery of all mysteries shrouded in the clouds, is nearest of the near, is your own Self, the reality of your life, body, and soul. tags.when_helps: Someone finding that sensory pleasures leave them empty and wondering where real happiness lies.

display_text: Happiness, we see is what everyone is seeking for, but the majority seek it in things which are evanescent and not real. No happiness was ever found in the senses. core_idea: Happiness is found only in the Spirit.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: As soon as I think that I am a little body, I want to preserve it, to protect it, to keep it nice, at the expense of other bodies; then you and I become separate. As soon as this idea of separation comes, it opens the door to all mischief and leads to all misery.
note: Selfishness and separation as the root of misery

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling cut off and defensive against others, open to seeing separateness as the root of misery.

display_text: As soon as I think that I am a little body, I want to preserve it, to protect it, to keep it nice, at the expense of other bodies; then you and I become separate. As soon as this idea of separation comes, it opens the door to all mischief and leads to all misery.
plain: As soon as I think I am just a small body, I want to protect and pamper it at others' expense, and you and I become separate. That idea of separation opens the door to all wrongdoing and all misery.
core_idea: Feeling separate from others causes all misery.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: There is a great tendency in modern times to talk too much of work and decry thought. Doing is very good, but that comes from thinking. Little manifestations of energy through the muscles are called work. But where there is no thought, there will be no work. Fill the brain, therefore, with high thoughts, highest ideals, place them day and night before you, and out of that will come great work.
note: Purpose and work grow from high ideals

tags.when_helps: Someone busy but directionless in their work, who needs to fill their mind with high ideals first.

display_text: There is a great tendency in modern times to talk too much of work and decry thought. Doing is very good, but that comes from thinking. Little manifestations of energy through the muscles are called work. But where there is no thought, there will be no work. Fill the brain, therefore, with high thoughts, highest ideals, place them day and night before you, and out of that will come great work.
plain: People today praise doing and look down on thinking, but all work comes from thought. So fill your mind with the highest thoughts and ideals, keep them before you day and night, and great work will follow.
core_idea: Great work grows from high thoughts.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: “Why weepest thou, my friend? There is neither birth nor death for thee. Why weepest thou? There is no disease nor misery for thee, but thou art like the infinite sky; clouds of various colours come over it, play for a moment, then vanish. But the sky is ever the same eternal blue.”
note: Sorrow passes like clouds; your deeper self untouched

tags.when_helps: Someone weeping over pain or illness who may find comfort in seeing troubles as clouds passing an unchanging sky.

display_text: “Why weepest thou, my friend? There is neither birth nor death for thee. Why weepest thou? There is no disease nor misery for thee, but thou art like the infinite sky; clouds of various colours come over it, play for a moment, then vanish. But the sky is ever the same eternal blue.”
plain: Why are you crying, friend? For you there is no birth or death, no disease or misery. You are like the endless sky: coloured clouds pass over it and vanish, but the sky stays the same eternal blue.
core_idea: You are the unchanging sky; troubles are passing clouds.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: There was a stump of a tree, and in the dark, a thief came that way and said, “That is a policeman.” A young man waiting for his beloved saw it and thought that it was his sweetheart. A child who had been told ghost stories took it for a ghost and began to shriek. But all the time it was the stump of a tree. We see the world as we are.
note: Fear and judgement project our inner state

keywords: we see the world as we are
tags.when_helps: Someone whose fears or hopes colour everything, ready to notice how much their mind shapes what they see.

display_text: There was a stump of a tree, and in the dark, a thief came that way and said, “That is a policeman.” A young man waiting for his beloved saw it and thought that it was his sweetheart. A child who had been told ghost stories took it for a ghost and began to shriek. But all the time it was the stump of a tree. We see the world as we are.
plain: In the dark, a thief took a tree stump for a policeman, a lover for his sweetheart, a child for a ghost. It was only a stump. We see the world as we are.
core_idea: We see the world as we are.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: Do not talk of the wickedness of the world and all its sins. Weep that you are bound to see wickedness yet. Weep that you are bound to see sin everywhere, and if you want to help the world, do not condemn it. Do not weaken it more.
note: Judging others; helping instead of condemning

tags.when_helps: Someone who sees wickedness everywhere and is tempted to condemn the world rather than help it.

display_text: Do not talk of the wickedness of the world and all its sins. Weep that you are bound to see wickedness yet. Weep that you are bound to see sin everywhere, and if you want to help the world, do not condemn it. Do not weaken it more.
plain: Don't talk about the world's wickedness and sin; grieve that you still see wickedness and sin everywhere. If you want to help the world, don't condemn it and make it weaker still.
core_idea: Help the world by not condemning it.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter II. The Real Nature Of Man
text: Let us be brave. Know the Truth and practice the Truth. The goal may be distant, but awake, arise, and stop not till the goal is reached.
note: Courage and perseverance toward a distant goal

tags.when_helps: Someone losing heart before a distant goal who needs a short, bracing call to keep going.

display_text: Let us be brave. Know the Truth and practice the Truth. The goal may be distant, but awake, arise, and stop not till the goal is reached.
plain: Let us be brave. Know the Truth and live it. The goal may be far away, but wake up, get up, and don't stop until you reach it.
core_idea: Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: Every child is a born optimist; he dreams golden dreams. In youth he becomes still more optimistic. It is hard for a young man to believe that there is such a thing as death, such a thing as defeat or degradation. Old age comes, and life is a mass of ruins. Dreams have vanished into the air, and the man becomes a pessimist. Thus we go from one extreme to another, buffeted by nature, without knowing where we are going.
note: Lost dreams; swinging between hope and despair with age

situations: loss of a dream or plan
tags.when_helps: Someone who has watched youthful dreams fade into disillusion and wants to see this as a common human arc.

display_text: Every child is a born optimist; he dreams golden dreams. In youth he becomes still more optimistic. It is hard for a young man to believe that there is such a thing as death, such a thing as defeat or degradation. Old age comes, and life is a mass of ruins. Dreams have vanished into the air, and the man becomes a pessimist. Thus we go from one extreme to another, buffeted by nature, without knowing where we are going.
plain: Children are born optimists, and youth hardly believes in death or defeat. Then old age comes, dreams vanish, and the person turns pessimist. Pushed by nature, we swing between extremes without knowing where we go.
core_idea: We swing from youthful hope to old despair.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: Death is stalking day and night over this earth of ours, but at the same time we think we shall live eternally. A question was once asked of King Yudhishthira, “What is the most wonderful thing on this earth?” And the king replied, “Every day people are dying around us, and yet men think they will never die.”
note: Denying our own mortality

tags.when_helps: Someone living as if they had forever, who could use a striking reminder of mortality to wake up.

display_text: Death is stalking day and night over this earth of ours, but at the same time we think we shall live eternally. A question was once asked of King Yudhishthira, “What is the most wonderful thing on this earth?” And the king replied, “Every day people are dying around us, and yet men think they will never die.”
plain: Death roams the earth day and night, yet we think we will live forever. Asked what the most wonderful thing on earth was, King Yudhishthira replied that people die around us every day, yet everyone thinks they will never die.
core_idea: We see death daily yet think we won't die.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: Hiding facts is not the way to find a remedy. As you all know, a hare hunted by dogs puts its head down and thinks itself safe; so, when we run into optimism; we do just like the hare, but that is no remedy.
note: Avoidance and denial instead of facing problems

tags.when_helps: Someone avoiding a hard truth by forced positivity, who needs a nudge to face facts honestly.

display_text: Hiding facts is not the way to find a remedy. As you all know, a hare hunted by dogs puts its head down and thinks itself safe; so, when we run into optimism; we do just like the hare, but that is no remedy.
plain: Hiding from facts is no remedy. A hare chased by dogs puts its head down and thinks it is safe; when we escape into optimism we do the same, but it solves nothing.
core_idea: Blind optimism is hiding, not a remedy.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: As we increase our power to be happy, we also increase our power to suffer, and sometimes I am inclined to think that if we increase our power to become happy in arithmetical progression, we shall increase, on the other hand, our power to become miserable in geometrical progression. We who are progressing know that the more we progress, the more avenues are opened to pain as well as to pleasure.
note: Greater sensitivity brings both more joy and more pain

tags.when_helps: Someone noticing that greater sensitivity brings both more joy and more pain, wanting to understand why.

display_text: As we increase our power to be happy, we also increase our power to suffer, and sometimes I am inclined to think that if we increase our power to become happy in arithmetical progression, we shall increase, on the other hand, our power to become miserable in geometrical progression. We who are progressing know that the more we progress, the more avenues are opened to pain as well as to pleasure.
plain: As our capacity for happiness grows, so does our capacity for suffering, perhaps even faster. The more we progress, the more doors open to pain as well as pleasure.
core_idea: Greater capacity for joy brings greater capacity for pain.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: We may verily imagine that there will be a place where there will be only good and no evil, where we shall only smile and never weep. This is impossible in the very nature of things; for the conditions will remain the same. Wherever there is the power of producing a smile in us, there lurks the power of producing tears. Wherever there is the power of producing happiness, there lurks somewhere the power of making us miserable.
note: Joy and sorrow come together; no life without tears

tags.when_helps: Someone longing for a life with only good and no pain, ready to accept that both come together.

display_text: We may verily imagine that there will be a place where there will be only good and no evil, where we shall only smile and never weep. This is impossible in the very nature of things; for the conditions will remain the same. Wherever there is the power of producing a smile in us, there lurks the power of producing tears. Wherever there is the power of producing happiness, there lurks somewhere the power of making us miserable.
plain: We may imagine a place of only good and no evil, only smiles and no tears, but that is impossible. Whatever can make us smile or happy can also make us cry or miserable.
core_idea: Whatever brings joy can also bring sorrow.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: What I thought to be good yesterday, I do not think to be good now. When I look back upon my life and see what were my ideals at different times, I final this to be so. At one time my ideal was to drive a strong pair of horses; at another time I thought, if I could make a certain kind of sweetmeat, I should be perfectly happy; later I imagined that I should be entirely satisfied if I had a wife and children and plenty of money. Today I laugh at all these ideals as mere childish nonsense.
note: Desires and ideals change as we grow

tags.when_helps: Someone sure that one particular thing will make them happy, reflecting on how their wants keep changing.

display_text: What I thought to be good yesterday, I do not think to be good now. When I look back upon my life and see what were my ideals at different times, I find this to be so. At one time my ideal was to drive a strong pair of horses; at another time I thought, if I could make a certain kind of sweetmeat, I should be perfectly happy; later I imagined that I should be entirely satisfied if I had a wife and children and plenty of money. Today I laugh at all these ideals as mere childish nonsense.
plain: What I thought good yesterday I no longer think good. Over my life my ideals changed: a fine pair of horses, a certain sweet, then a wife, children and money. Today I laugh at them all as childish nonsense.
core_idea: Our ideals keep changing as we grow.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: There comes a time when the mind awakes from this long and dreary dream — the child gives up its play and wants to go back to its mother. It finds the truth of the statement, “Desire is never satisfied by the enjoyment of desires, it only increases the more, as fire, when butter is poured upon it.”
note: Desire is never satisfied by indulging it

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone worn out by indulging desires that only grow stronger, ready to wake from the cycle.

display_text: There comes a time when the mind awakes from this long and dreary dream — the child gives up its play and wants to go back to its mother. It finds the truth of the statement, “Desire is never satisfied by the enjoyment of desires, it only increases the more, as fire, when butter is poured upon it.”
plain: A time comes when the mind wakes from its long, dreary dream, like a child leaving play to go back to its mother. It learns that indulging desire only feeds it, as butter feeds a fire.
core_idea: Indulging desire only feeds it, like fire.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: Fanatics cannot work, they waste three-fourths of their energy. It is the level-headed, calm, practical man who works.
note: Calm, not zeal, gets real work done

tags.when_helps: Someone spending energy on zeal or agitation who needs a reminder that calm, practical people get things done.

display_text: Fanatics cannot work, they waste three-fourths of their energy. It is the level-headed, calm, practical man who works.
plain: Fanatics can't really work; they waste three-quarters of their energy. It is the calm, level-headed, practical person who gets work done.
core_idea: Calm, practical people work; fanatics waste energy.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter III. Maya And Illusion
text: The man who says that he will work when the world has become all good and then he will enjoy bliss is as likely to succeed as the man who sits beside the Ganga and says, “I will ford the river when all the water has run into the ocean.”
note: Waiting for perfect conditions before acting

tags.when_helps: Someone waiting for perfect conditions before acting, who needs to start now in an imperfect world.

display_text: The man who says that he will work when the world has become all good and then he will enjoy bliss is as likely to succeed as the man who sits beside the Ganga and says, “I will ford the river when all the water has run into the ocean.”
plain: Someone who says he will work and be happy once the world becomes entirely good is like a man sitting by the Ganges saying he will cross once all the water has flowed into the sea.
core_idea: Waiting for a perfect world means never acting.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IV. Maya And The Evolution Of The Conception Of God
text: In judging others we always judge them by our own ideals. That is not as it should be. Everyone must be judged according to his own ideal, and not by that of anyone else. In our dealings with our fellow-beings we constantly labour under this mistake, and I am of opinion that the vast majority of our quarrels with one another arise simply from this one cause that we are always trying to judge others’ gods by our own, others’ ideals by our ideals, and others’ motives by our motives. Under certain circumstances I might do a certain thing, and when I see another person taking the same course I think he has also the same motive actuating him, little dreaming that although the effect may be the same, yet many other causes may produce the same thing. He may have performed the action with quite a different motive from that which impelled me to do it.
note: Judging others' motives; quarrels and misunderstanding

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone in a quarrel who assumes they know the other's motives, open to seeing things from their side.

display_text: In judging others we always judge them by our own ideals. That is not as it should be. Everyone must be judged according to his own ideal, and not by that of anyone else. In our dealings with our fellow-beings we constantly labour under this mistake, and I am of opinion that the vast majority of our quarrels with one another arise simply from this one cause that we are always trying to judge others’ gods by our own, others’ ideals by our ideals, and others’ motives by our motives. Under certain circumstances I might do a certain thing, and when I see another person taking the same course I think he has also the same motive actuating him, little dreaming that although the effect may be the same, yet many other causes may produce the same thing. He may have performed the action with quite a different motive from that which impelled me to do it.
plain: We judge others by our own ideals, but everyone should be judged by theirs. Most quarrels come from judging others' gods, ideals and motives by our own. Someone may do what I would do for an entirely different reason.
core_idea: Judge others by their ideals, not yours.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IV. Maya And The Evolution Of The Conception Of God
text: There is one impulse in our minds which says, do. Behind it rises another voice which says, do not. There is one set of ideas in our mind which is always struggling to get outside through the channels of the senses, and behind that, although it may be thin and weak, there is an infinitely small voice which says, do not go outside.
note: Temptation and the quiet inner voice of restraint

tags.when_helps: Someone torn between impulse and an inner voice of restraint, wanting to understand that tension.

display_text: There is one impulse in our minds which says, do. Behind it rises another voice which says, do not. There is one set of ideas in our mind which is always struggling to get outside through the channels of the senses, and behind that, although it may be thin and weak, there is an infinitely small voice which says, do not go outside.
plain: One impulse in the mind says 'do', and behind it another voice says 'don't'. Our ideas constantly push outward through the senses, but behind them a tiny, faint voice says 'don't go outside'.
core_idea: A quiet inner voice pulls us back from the senses.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IV. Maya And The Evolution Of The Conception Of God
text: How can we live together without bearing and forbearing? How can one man live with another without having some time or other to check his impulses, to restrain himself, to forbear from doing things which his mind would prompt him to do? It is impossible. Thus comes the idea of restraint. The whole social fabric is based upon that idea of restraint, and we all know that the man or woman who has not learnt the great lesson of bearing and forbearing leads a most miserable life.
note: Patience and restraint in living with others

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone struggling to live peacefully with others who needs a reminder that restraint makes shared life possible.

display_text: How can we live together without bearing and forbearing? How can one man live with another without having some time or other to check his impulses, to restrain himself, to forbear from doing things which his mind would prompt him to do? It is impossible. Thus comes the idea of restraint. The whole social fabric is based upon that idea of restraint, and we all know that the man or woman who has not learnt the great lesson of bearing and forbearing leads a most miserable life.
plain: We cannot live together without putting up with each other and holding ourselves back. All society rests on restraint, and anyone who hasn't learned to bear and forbear lives a very miserable life.
core_idea: Living together requires bearing and forbearing.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IV. Maya And The Evolution Of The Conception Of God
text: Here we are with strong impulses and stronger cravings for sense-enjoyments, but cannot satisfy them. There rises a wave which impels us forward in spite of our own will, and as soon as we move one step, comes a blow. We are all doomed to live here like Tantalus. Ideals come into our head far beyond the limit of our sense-ideals, but when we seek to express them, we cannot do so. On the other hand, we are crushed by the surging mass around us. Yet if I give up all ideality and merely struggle through this world, my existence is that of a brute, and I degenerate and degrade myself. Neither way is happiness.
note: Frustrated cravings and ideals; feeling stuck

tags.when_helps: Someone caught between unmet cravings and unreachable ideals, feeling neither path brings happiness.

display_text: Here we are with strong impulses and stronger cravings for sense-enjoyments, but cannot satisfy them. There rises a wave which impels us forward in spite of our own will, and as soon as we move one step, comes a blow. We are all doomed to live here like Tantalus. Ideals come into our head far beyond the limit of our sense-ideals, but when we seek to express them, we cannot do so. On the other hand, we are crushed by the surging mass around us. Yet if I give up all ideality and merely struggle through this world, my existence is that of a brute, and I degenerate and degrade myself. Neither way is happiness.
plain: We have strong cravings we can't satisfy; every step forward brings a blow, like Tantalus. Our high ideals can't find expression and the crowd crushes us. Yet giving up ideals to just survive makes us brutish. Neither way brings happiness.
core_idea: Neither chasing nor abandoning ideals brings happiness.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IV. Maya And The Evolution Of The Conception Of God
text: What you do not make free, will never grow. The idea that you can make others grow and help their growth, that you can direct and guide them, always retaining for yourself the freedom of the teacher, is nonsense, a dangerous lie which has retarded the growth of millions and millions of human beings in this world. Let men have the light of liberty. That is the only condition of growth.
note: Controlling others versus giving them freedom to grow

tags.when_helps: A parent, teacher or manager tempted to control others' growth, reminded that freedom is the condition of growth.

display_text: What you do not make free, will never grow. The idea that you can make others grow and help their growth, that you can direct and guide them, always retaining for yourself the freedom of the teacher, is nonsense, a dangerous lie which has retarded the growth of millions and millions of human beings in this world. Let men have the light of liberty. That is the only condition of growth.
plain: What you don't set free will never grow. Thinking you can guide others' growth while keeping all freedom for yourself is a dangerous lie that has held back millions. Liberty is the only condition of growth.
core_idea: Freedom is the only condition of growth.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IV. Maya And The Evolution Of The Conception Of God
text: Suppose there is an evil; denouncing it will not remove it, but you must go to work at the root. First find out the cause, then remove it, and the effect will be removed also.
note: Fixing problems at the root instead of complaining

tags.when_helps: Someone angry at a wrong who wants to fix its cause rather than only denounce it.

display_text: Suppose there is an evil; denouncing it will not remove it, but you must go to work at the root. First find out the cause, then remove it, and the effect will be removed also.
plain: Denouncing an evil won't remove it. Go to the root: find the cause and remove it, and the effect will go too.
core_idea: Remove the cause, not just denounce the evil.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IV. Maya And The Evolution Of The Conception Of God
text: He who sees in this world of manifoldness that One running through all, in this world of death he who finds that One Infinite Life, and in this world of insentience and ignorance he who finds that One Light and Knowledge, unto him belongs eternal peace. Unto none else, unto none else.
note: Finding peace by seeing unity beneath everything

tags.when_helps: A seeker longing for lasting peace amid a world of change and death.

display_text: He who sees in this world of manifoldness that One running through all, in this world of death he who finds that One Infinite Life, and in this world of insentience and ignorance he who finds that One Light and Knowledge, unto him belongs eternal peace. Unto none else, unto none else.
plain: Whoever sees the One running through this world of many things, finds the One Infinite Life in this world of death, and the One Light in this world of ignorance, has eternal peace, and no one else.
core_idea: Eternal peace belongs to those who see the One.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter V. Maya And Freedom
text: We come here weeping to fight our way, as well as we can, and to make a path for ourselves through this infinite ocean of life; forward we go, having long ages behind us and an immense expanse beyond. So on we go, till death comes and takes us off the field — victorious or defeated, we do not know.
note: Life as a struggle with uncertain outcome

tags.when_helps: Someone struggling through life without knowing if they are winning, needing to feel this is everyone's lot.

display_text: We come here weeping to fight our way, as well as we can, and to make a path for ourselves through this infinite ocean of life; forward we go, having long ages behind us and an immense expanse beyond. So on we go, till death comes and takes us off the field — victorious or defeated, we do not know.
plain: We arrive crying and fight our way through life's endless ocean as best we can, with ages behind us and vast stretches ahead, until death takes us off the field, and we don't know whether we won or lost.
core_idea: We struggle through life not knowing if we win.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter V. Maya And Freedom
text: Man is seeking for pleasure and for happiness where it can never be found. For countless ages we are all taught that this is futile and vain, there is no happiness here. But we cannot learn; it is impossible for us to do so, except through our own experiences. We try them, and a blow comes. Do we learn then? Not even then. Like moths hurling themselves against the flame, we are hurling ourselves again and again into sense-pleasures, hoping to find satisfaction there. We return again and again with freshened energy; thus we go on, till crippled and cheated we die.
note: Repeating the same mistakes chasing pleasure

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone repeatedly chasing pleasures that hurt them, ready for a blunt picture of the pattern.

display_text: Man is seeking for pleasure and for happiness where it can never be found. For countless ages we are all taught that this is futile and vain, there is no happiness here. But we cannot learn; it is impossible for us to do so, except through our own experiences. We try them, and a blow comes. Do we learn then? Not even then. Like moths hurling themselves against the flame, we are hurling ourselves again and again into sense-pleasures, hoping to find satisfaction there. We return again and again with freshened energy; thus we go on, till crippled and cheated we die.
plain: We seek happiness where it can't be found. Though told for ages it is futile, we learn only by experience, and not even then. Like moths into a flame we keep hurling ourselves at sense pleasures until we die cheated.
core_idea: Like moths, we keep chasing pleasures that burn us.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter V. Maya And Freedom
text: We cannot hide a carrion with roses; it is impossible. It would not avail long; for soon the roses would fade, and the carrion would be worse than ever before. So with our lives. We may try to cover our old and festering sores with cloth of gold, but there comes a day when the cloth of gold is removed, and the sore in all its ugliness is revealed.
note: Denial; covering over pain instead of facing it

tags.when_helps: Someone covering up a deep problem with appearances, who needs to hear it will surface and must be faced.

display_text: We cannot hide a carrion with roses; it is impossible. It would not avail long; for soon the roses would fade, and the carrion would be worse than ever before. So with our lives. We may try to cover our old and festering sores with cloth of gold, but there comes a day when the cloth of gold is removed, and the sore in all its ugliness is revealed.
plain: You can't hide rotting flesh under roses for long; the roses fade and it is worse than before. So with our lives: we may cover festering sores with gold cloth, but one day it is removed.
core_idea: You cannot hide decay for long.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter V. Maya And Freedom
text: The beautiful, hopeful, young person of today is the veteran of tomorrow. Hopes and joys and pleasures will die like blossoms with tomorrow’s frost.
note: Ageing and the impermanence of pleasures

tags.when_helps: Someone sensing youth and joy slipping away, wanting honest words about how all things pass.

display_text: The beautiful, hopeful, young person of today is the veteran of tomorrow. Hopes and joys and pleasures will die like blossoms with tomorrow’s frost.
plain: Today's beautiful, hopeful young person is tomorrow's old veteran. Hopes, joys and pleasures will die like blossoms in tomorrow's frost.
core_idea: Youth and its joys fade like blossoms.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter V. Maya And Freedom
text: One stumbles more than another, and him who stumbles more we call bad, him who stumbles less we call good. Good and bad are never two different things, they are one and the same; the difference is not one of kind, but of degree.
note: Judging self and others; failure as stumbling

tags.when_helps: Someone judging themselves or others as bad, open to seeing everyone as stumbling by degrees.

display_text: One stumbles more than another, and him who stumbles more we call bad, him who stumbles less we call good. Good and bad are never two different things, they are one and the same; the difference is not one of kind, but of degree.
plain: One person stumbles more than another; we call the one who stumbles more bad and the one who stumbles less good. Good and bad are not different things but the same, differing only in degree.
core_idea: Good and bad differ in degree, not kind.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VI. The Absolute And Manifestation
text: The little fish wants to fly from its enemies in the water. How does it do so? By evolving wings and becoming a bird. The fish did not change the water or the air; the change was in itself. Change is always subjective.
note: Changing yourself rather than your circumstances

tags.when_helps: Someone wishing their circumstances would change, ready to consider changing themselves instead.

display_text: The little fish wants to fly from its enemies in the water. How does it do so? By evolving wings and becoming a bird. The fish did not change the water or the air; the change was in itself. Change is always subjective.
plain: A small fish fleeing enemies in the water escaped by growing wings and becoming a bird. It didn't change the water or the air; it changed itself. Change always happens within.
core_idea: Real change comes from within.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: The heart is great indeed; it is through the heart that come the great inspirations of life. I would a hundred times rather have a little heart and no brain, than be all brains and no heart. Life is possible, progress is possible for him who has heart, but he who has no heart and only brains dies of dryness. At the same time we know that he who is carried along by his heart alone has to undergo many ills, for now and then he is liable to tumble into pitfalls. The combination of heart and head is what we want.
note: Balancing feeling and reason in life and decisions

tags.when_helps: Someone torn between feeling and reason, or drying out from overthinking, who needs both in balance.

display_text: The heart is great indeed; it is through the heart that come the great inspirations of life. I would a hundred times rather have a little heart and no brain, than be all brains and no heart. Life is possible, progress is possible for him who has heart, but he who has no heart and only brains dies of dryness. At the same time we know that he who is carried along by his heart alone has to undergo many ills, for now and then he is liable to tumble into pitfalls. The combination of heart and head is what we want.
plain: Life's great inspirations come through the heart. Better a little heart and no brain than all brain and no heart, which withers. Yet heart alone falls into pitfalls; we need heart and head together.
core_idea: We need heart and head together.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: In life and in death, in happiness and in misery, the Lord is equally present. The whole world is full of the Lord. Open your eyes and see Him.
note: Finding the sacred in both joy and suffering

tags.when_helps: A believer in hardship who wants to be reminded that God is present in misery as in joy.

display_text: In life and in death, in happiness and in misery, the Lord is equally present. The whole world is full of the Lord. Open your eyes and see Him.
plain: The Lord is equally present in life and death, in happiness and misery. The whole world is full of the Lord. Open your eyes and see Him.
core_idea: The Lord is present everywhere; open your eyes.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: What makes us miserable? The cause of all miseries from which we suffer is desire. You desire something, and the desire is not fulfilled; the result is distress. If there is no desire, there is no suffering.
note: Disappointment; unmet desire as the root of distress

tags.when_helps: Someone distressed by an unfulfilled want, willing to see the desire itself as the source of suffering.

display_text: What makes us miserable? The cause of all miseries from which we suffer is desire. You desire something, and the desire is not fulfilled; the result is distress. If there is no desire, there is no suffering.
plain: What makes us miserable? Desire causes all our suffering. You want something, don't get it, and you are distressed. Without desire there is no suffering.
core_idea: Desire is the cause of all suffering.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: There are hundreds of things we have done in our lives which we wish we had never done, but which, at the same time, have been great teachers. As for me, I am glad I have done something good and many things bad; glad I have done something right, and glad I have committed many errors, because every one of them has been a great lesson. I, as I am now, am the resultant of all I have done, all I have thought.
note: Regret; mistakes as teachers

tags.when_helps: Someone haunted by past mistakes who could see them as lessons that made them who they are.

display_text: There are hundreds of things we have done in our lives which we wish we had never done, but which, at the same time, have been great teachers. As for me, I am glad I have done something good and many things bad; glad I have done something right, and glad I have committed many errors, because every one of them has been a great lesson. I, as I am now, am the resultant of all I have done, all I have thought.
plain: We've done many things we wish we hadn't, yet they taught us much. I'm glad of my good deeds and my many mistakes, since each was a lesson. I am the result of all I have done and thought.
core_idea: Our mistakes are lessons; we are their sum.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: “The kingdom of heaven is within you,” says Jesus; so says the Vedanta, and every great teacher. “He that hath eyes to see, let him see, and he that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” The Vedanta proves that the truth for which we have been searching all this time is present, and was all the time with us. In our ignorance, we thought we had lost it, and went about the world crying and weeping, struggling to find the truth, while all along it was dwelling in our own hearts. There alone can we find it.
note: Searching outward for what lies within

tags.when_helps: Someone weary of searching for truth outside who needs to hear it has been within them all along.

display_text: “The kingdom of heaven is within you,” says Jesus; so says the Vedanta, and every great teacher. “He that hath eyes to see, let him see, and he that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” The Vedanta proves that the truth for which we have been searching all this time is present, and was all the time with us. In our ignorance, we thought we had lost it, and went about the world crying and weeping, struggling to find the truth, while all along it was dwelling in our own hearts. There alone can we find it.
plain: Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is within you, and so do the Vedanta and every great teacher. In ignorance we roamed the world weeping for the truth, while it lived all along in our own hearts.
core_idea: The truth we seek is within our hearts.

plain_judge.issue: Drops 'there alone can we find it' and the eyes-to-see saying.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: Who enjoys the picture, the seller or the seer? The seller is busy with his accounts, computing what his gain will be, how much profit he will realise on the picture. His brain is full of that. He is looking at the hammer, and watching the bids. He is intent on hearing how fast the bids are rising. That man is enjoying the picture who has gone there without any intention of buying or selling. He looks at the picture and enjoys it.
note: Possessiveness and gain spoil enjoyment of life

tags.when_helps: Someone so focused on gain that they no longer enjoy things, reminded that delight comes without wanting to own.

display_text: Who enjoys the picture, the seller or the seer? The seller is busy with his accounts, computing what his gain will be, how much profit he will realise on the picture. His brain is full of that. He is looking at the hammer, and watching the bids. He is intent on hearing how fast the bids are rising. That man is enjoying the picture who has gone there without any intention of buying or selling. He looks at the picture and enjoys it.
plain: Who enjoys a painting, the seller or the viewer? The seller is busy counting his profit and watching the bids. The one who enjoys it is the person who came with no intention of buying or selling and simply looks.
core_idea: Only those who want nothing truly enjoy.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: If a man plunges headlong into foolish luxuries of the world without knowing the truth, he has missed his footing, he cannot reach the goal. And if a man curses the world, goes into a forest, mortifies his flesh, and kills himself little by little by starvation, makes his heart a barren waste, kills out all feelings, and becomes harsh, stern, and dried-up, that man also has missed the way. These are the two extremes, the two mistakes at either end. Both have lost the way, both have missed the goal.
note: Avoiding both indulgence and harsh self-denial

tags.when_helps: Someone swinging between indulgence and harsh self-denial, who needs to hear both extremes miss the way.

display_text: If a man plunges headlong into foolish luxuries of the world without knowing the truth, he has missed his footing, he cannot reach the goal. And if a man curses the world, goes into a forest, mortifies his flesh, and kills himself little by little by starvation, makes his heart a barren waste, kills out all feelings, and becomes harsh, stern, and dried-up, that man also has missed the way. These are the two extremes, the two mistakes at either end. Both have lost the way, both have missed the goal.
plain: Plunging into foolish luxury without knowing the truth misses the goal. So does cursing the world, fleeing to a forest and starving body and feeling until you are harsh and dried up. Both extremes lose the way.
core_idea: Both indulgence and harsh self-denial miss the goal.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: We are dying of thirst sitting on the banks of the mightiest river. We are dying of hunger sitting near heaps of food. Here is the blissful universe, yet we do not find it. We are in it all the time, and we are always mistaking it.
note: Missing the joy already around us

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling deprived while surrounded by blessing, ready to notice what is already there.

display_text: We are dying of thirst sitting on the banks of the mightiest river. We are dying of hunger sitting near heaps of food. Here is the blissful universe, yet we do not find it. We are in it all the time, and we are always mistaking it.
plain: We are dying of thirst beside the mightiest river and of hunger beside heaps of food. The universe is full of bliss, yet we are in it all the time and keep mistaking it.
core_idea: Bliss surrounds us, yet we fail to see it.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: It is very easy to talk. From my childhood I have heard of seeing God everywhere and in everything, and then I can really enjoy the world, but as soon as I mix with the world, and get a few blows from it, the idea vanishes. I am walking in the street thinking that God is in every man, and a strong man comes along and gives me a push and I fall flat on the footpath. Then I rise up quickly with clenched fist, the blood has rushed to my head, and the reflection goes. Immediately I have become mad. Everything is forgotten; instead of encountering God I see the devil.
note: Ideals vanishing in a flash of anger

tags.when_helps: Someone whose spiritual ideals evaporate the moment they are provoked, comforted that even a teacher struggles.

display_text: It is very easy to talk. From my childhood I have heard of seeing God everywhere and in everything, and then I can really enjoy the world, but as soon as I mix with the world, and get a few blows from it, the idea vanishes. I am walking in the street thinking that God is in every man, and a strong man comes along and gives me a push and I fall flat on the footpath. Then I rise up quickly with clenched fist, the blood has rushed to my head, and the reflection goes. Immediately I have become mad. Everything is forgotten; instead of encountering God I see the devil.
plain: It's easy to talk about seeing God in everyone. But when a strong man shoves me onto the pavement, I jump up with clenched fists, the thought gone. Instead of meeting God, I see the devil.
core_idea: Seeing God in everyone vanishes at the first shove.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: You all remember how in Æesop’s Fables a fine stag is looking at his form reflected in a lake and is saying to his young one, “How powerful I am, look at my splendid head, look at my limbs, how strong and muscular they are; and how swiftly I can run.” In the meantime he hears the barking of dogs in the distance, and immediately takes to his heels, and after he has run several miles, he comes back panting. The young one says, “You just told me how strong you were, how was it that when the dog barked, you ran away?” “Yes, my son; but when the dogs bark all my confidence vanishes.” Such is the case with us. We think highly of humanity, we feel ourselves strong and valiant, we make grand resolves; but when the “dogs” of trial and temptation bark, we are like the stag in the fable.
note: Confidence and resolve collapsing under trial

tags.when_helps: Someone whose confidence collapses under trial or temptation, recognising this as a shared human weakness.

display_text: You all remember how in Æsop’s Fables a fine stag is looking at his form reflected in a lake and is saying to his young one, “How powerful I am, look at my splendid head, look at my limbs, how strong and muscular they are; and how swiftly I can run.” In the meantime he hears the barking of dogs in the distance, and immediately takes to his heels, and after he has run several miles, he comes back panting. The young one says, “You just told me how strong you were, how was it that when the dog barked, you ran away?” “Yes, my son; but when the dogs bark all my confidence vanishes.” Such is the case with us. We think highly of humanity, we feel ourselves strong and valiant, we make grand resolves; but when the “dogs” of trial and temptation bark, we are like the stag in the fable.
plain: In Aesop's fable, a stag boasts of his strength, then flees when dogs bark; his confidence vanishes at the sound. We are the same: bold in our resolutions, but we run when trial and temptation bark.
core_idea: Our confidence vanishes when trials come.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: Unfortunately in this life, the vast majority of persons are groping through this dark life without any ideal at all. If a man with an ideal makes a thousand mistakes, I am sure that the man without an ideal makes fifty thousand. Therefore, it is better to have an ideal.
note: Purpose; having an ideal despite mistakes

tags.when_helps: Someone drifting without direction who needs encouragement to choose an ideal, even imperfectly.

display_text: Unfortunately in this life, the vast majority of persons are groping through this dark life without any ideal at all. If a man with an ideal makes a thousand mistakes, I am sure that the man without an ideal makes fifty thousand. Therefore, it is better to have an ideal.
plain: Most people grope through life with no ideal at all. If someone with an ideal makes a thousand mistakes, someone without one makes fifty thousand. So it is better to have an ideal.
core_idea: Better to have an ideal, even with mistakes.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VII. God In Everything
text: Never mind failures; they are quite natural, they are the beauty of life, these failures. What would life be without them? It would not be worth having if it were not for struggles. Where would be the poetry of life? Never mind the struggles, the mistakes. I never heard a cow tell a lie, but it is only a cow — never a man. So never mind these failures, these little backslidings; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.
note: Failure and trying again

tags.when_helps: Someone discouraged by repeated failure who needs to hear failures are natural and to try once more.

display_text: Never mind failures; they are quite natural, they are the beauty of life, these failures. What would life be without them? It would not be worth having if it were not for struggles. Where would be the poetry of life? Never mind the struggles, the mistakes. I never heard a cow tell a lie, but it is only a cow — never a man. So never mind these failures, these little backslidings; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.
plain: Don't mind failures; they are natural, the beauty and poetry of life, which would be worthless without struggle. Only a cow never lies. Hold to your ideal, and if you fail a thousand times, try once more.
core_idea: Fail a thousand times, then try once more.

plain_judge.issue: 'Only a cow never lies' loses the point that only a cow, never a man, is faultless.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: Nachiketas said, “These are merely things of a day, O Death, they wear away the energy of all the sense-organs. Even the longest life is very short. These horses and chariots, dances and songs, may remain with Thee. Man cannot be satisfied by wealth. Can we retain wealth when we behold Thee? We shall live only so long as Thou desires”.
note: Wealth and pleasure cannot satisfy; life is short

tags.when_helps: Someone offered wealth or pleasure who senses it will not satisfy and wants something deeper.

display_text: Nachiketas said, “These are merely things of a day, O Death, they wear away the energy of all the sense-organs. Even the longest life is very short. These horses and chariots, dances and songs, may remain with Thee. Man cannot be satisfied by wealth. Can we retain wealth when we behold Thee? We shall live only so long as Thou desires”.
plain: Nachiketas told Death: these pleasures last a day and wear out the senses, and even the longest life is short. Keep your horses, chariots, dances and songs. Wealth cannot satisfy a person, nor can we keep it when we face you; we live only as long as you wish.
core_idea: Wealth and pleasure cannot satisfy a human being

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: If you have seen a certain country, and a man forces you to say that you have not seen it, still in your heart of hearts you know you have. So, when you see religion and God in a more intense sense than you see this external world, nothing will be able to shake your belief. Then you have real faith.
note: Faith grounded in direct experience, not argument

tags.when_helps: Someone with shaky belief who wants to understand faith as direct experience rather than argument.

display_text: If you have seen a certain country, and a man forces you to say that you have not seen it, still in your heart of hearts you know you have. So, when you see religion and God in a more intense sense than you see this external world, nothing will be able to shake your belief. Then you have real faith.
plain: Once you see religion and God more vividly than you see the outside world, nothing can shake your belief, just as no one can make you doubt a country you have visited. That is real faith.
core_idea: Real faith comes from direct experience of God

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: What is joy, and what is sorrow? It is a vanishing quantity, continually vanishing. When I was a child I thought if I could be a cabman, it would be the very acme of happiness for me to drive about. I do not think so now. To what joy will you cling?
note: Changing ideas of happiness; clinging to pleasures

tags.when_helps: Someone clinging to a particular joy, reflecting on how quickly what pleases us changes.

display_text: What is joy, and what is sorrow? It is a vanishing quantity, continually vanishing. When I was a child I thought if I could be a cabman, it would be the very acme of happiness for me to drive about. I do not think so now. To what joy will you cling?
plain: Joy and sorrow keep vanishing: as a child he thought driving a cab would be perfect happiness, and now he does not. So which joy will you cling to?
core_idea: Every joy we chase keeps changing and vanishing

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: The very thing I call pleasurable today, tomorrow under better circumstances I may call pain. The fire that warms us can also consume us; it is not the fault of the fire.
note: Pleasure and pain as two sides of one thing

tags.when_helps: Someone hurt by something that once brought pleasure, seeing that the same thing can bring both.

display_text: The very thing I call pleasurable today, tomorrow under better circumstances I may call pain. The fire that warms us can also consume us; it is not the fault of the fire.
plain: What feels like pleasure today may feel like pain tomorrow. The same fire that warms us can burn us, and that is not the fire's fault.
core_idea: The same thing can bring pleasure or pain

plain_judge.issue: Drops 'under better circumstances', a small loss of nuance.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: Picture the Self to be then rider and this body the chariot, the intellect to be the charioteer, mind the reins, and the senses the horses. He whose horses are well broken, and whose reins are strong and kept well in the hands of the charioteer (the intellect) reaches the goal which is the state of Him, the Omnipresent. But the man whose horses (the senses) are not controlled, nor the reins (the mind) well managed, goes to destruction.
note: Self-control; mastering impulses and the senses

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone pulled around by their senses who wants a clear image for steering their mind with intellect.

display_text: Picture the Self to be then rider and this body the chariot, the intellect to be the charioteer, mind the reins, and the senses the horses. He whose horses are well broken, and whose reins are strong and kept well in the hands of the charioteer (the intellect) reaches the goal which is the state of Him, the Omnipresent. But the man whose horses (the senses) are not controlled, nor the reins (the mind) well managed, goes to destruction.
plain: Picture the Self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as driver, the mind as reins and the senses as horses. Keep senses and mind in control and you reach God; lose control and you are destroyed.
core_idea: Control the senses and mind to reach the goal

plain_judge.issue: Simplifies the intellect's role and 'the state of the Omnipresent' to 'reach God'.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: It is, as it were, walking on the edge of a razor; the way is long and perilous, but struggle on, do not despair. Awake, arise, and stop not till the goal is reached.
note: Persevering on a hard path; not despairing

tags.when_helps: Someone on a long, perilous road who is close to giving up and needs urging not to despair.

display_text: It is, as it were, walking on the edge of a razor; the way is long and perilous, but struggle on, do not despair. Awake, arise, and stop not till the goal is reached.
plain: The path is like walking on a razor's edge, long and dangerous, but keep going and do not lose heart. Wake up, get up, and do not stop until you reach the goal.
core_idea: Keep striving on the hard path until the goal

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: If one thing is obvious to me it is this that desires bring all misery; it is the state of the beggar, who is always begging for something, and unable to see anything without the wish to possess it, is always longing, longing for more. If the power to satisfy our desires is increased in arithmetical progression, the power of desire is increased in geometrical progression.
note: Endless wanting; desire outpaces satisfaction

tags.when_helps: Someone always wanting more who is ready to see endless desire as the source of their misery.

display_text: If one thing is obvious to me it is this that desires bring all misery; it is the state of the beggar, who is always begging for something, and unable to see anything without the wish to possess it, is always longing, longing for more. If the power to satisfy our desires is increased in arithmetical progression, the power of desire is increased in geometrical progression.
plain: Desire causes all misery: it keeps you like a beggar, always wanting more. As your power to satisfy desires grows steadily, the desires themselves multiply far faster.
core_idea: Desire always outgrows our power to satisfy it

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter VIII. Realisation
text: Renunciation is the very basis of our true life; every moment of goodness and real life that we enjoy is when we do not think of ourselves. This little separate self must die.
note: Selflessness; joy in forgetting oneself

tags.when_helps: Someone sensing their best moments come when they forget themselves, open to loosening self-concern.

display_text: Renunciation is the very basis of our true life; every moment of goodness and real life that we enjoy is when we do not think of ourselves. This little separate self must die.
plain: Giving up the self is the basis of true life; every good and truly alive moment comes when we are not thinking of ourselves. The small, separate self has to die.
core_idea: True life comes from forgetting the separate self

plain_judge.issue: 'Renunciation' narrowed to 'giving up the self'; slight loss of breadth.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: In this world we find that all happiness is followed by misery as its shadow. Life has its shadow, death. They must go together, because they are not contradictory, not two separate existences, but different manifestations of the same unit, life and death, sorrow and happiness, good and evil.
note: Joy and sorrow, life and death, always together

tags.when_helps: Someone troubled that joy is always followed by sorrow, seeking to accept them as one whole.

display_text: In this world we find that all happiness is followed by misery as its shadow. Life has its shadow, death. They must go together, because they are not contradictory, not two separate existences, but different manifestations of the same unit, life and death, sorrow and happiness, good and evil.
plain: In this world, misery follows every happiness like a shadow, and death follows life. They belong together because they are not opposites but two sides of one thing, as are sorrow and joy, good and evil.
core_idea: Happiness and misery are two sides of one thing

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: I remember when I was young, a young man’s father died and left him poorly off, with a large family to support, and he found that his father ’s friends were unwilling to help him. He had a conversation with a clergyman who offered this consolation, “Oh, it is all good, all is sent for our good.” That is the old method of trying to put a piece of gold leaf on an old sore. It is a confession of weakness, of absurdity.
note: Grief and hollow consolations

tags.when_helps: Someone tired of hollow comfort like 'it's all for the good' who wants their hardship acknowledged honestly.

display_text: I remember when I was young, a young man’s father died and left him poorly off, with a large family to support, and he found that his father’s friends were unwilling to help him. He had a conversation with a clergyman who offered this consolation, “Oh, it is all good, all is sent for our good.” That is the old method of trying to put a piece of gold leaf on an old sore. It is a confession of weakness, of absurdity.
plain: A young man left poor after his father died was told by a clergyman that everything happens for our good. Such comfort is like gold leaf over an old sore: an admission of weakness and absurdity.
core_idea: Saying all suffering is good is empty comfort

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: Be good and have mercy on those who suffer. Do not try to patch it up, nothing will cure this world; go beyond it.
note: Compassion for suffering without false fixes

tags.when_helps: Someone exhausted by trying to fix the world's suffering, who needs a call to kindness and a higher aim.

display_text: Be good and have mercy on those who suffer. Do not try to patch it up, nothing will cure this world; go beyond it.
plain: Be good and show mercy to those who suffer. But do not try to patch the world up, because nothing will cure it; go beyond it.
core_idea: Be kind, but seek to go beyond the world

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: This life is a hard fact; work your way through it boldly, though it may be adamantine; no matter, the soul is stronger.
note: Courage in hardship

tags.when_helps: Someone facing a hard, unyielding situation who needs to hear they are stronger than it.

display_text: This life is a hard fact; work your way through it boldly, though it may be adamantine; no matter, the soul is stronger.
plain: Life is hard and real; push through it bravely, however unyielding it seems. It does not matter, because the soul is stronger.
core_idea: The soul is stronger than life's hardships

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: You make yourselves suffer, you make good and evil, and it is you who put your hands before your eyes and say it is dark. Take your hands away and see the light; you are effulgent, you are perfect already, from the very beginning.
note: Self-made darkness; seeing one's own worth

tags.when_helps: Someone convinced all is dark, open to the idea that they are already whole and can see light.

display_text: You make yourselves suffer, you make good and evil, and it is you who put your hands before your eyes and say it is dark. Take your hands away and see the light; you are effulgent, you are perfect already, from the very beginning.
plain: You cause your own suffering and make good and evil; you cover your eyes and complain it is dark. Take your hands away and see the light: you are radiant and already perfect, and always were.
core_idea: You are already perfect; stop covering your eyes

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: Changing places does not help one much. I thought while I was in India that the cave would give me clearer vision. I found it was not so. Then I thought the forest would do so, then, Varanasi. But the same difficulty existed everywhere, because we make our own worlds. If I am evil, the whole world is evil to me.
note: Running away; we carry our troubles with us

tags.when_helps: Someone hoping a new place will fix their troubles, reminded that they bring their inner world with them.

display_text: Changing places does not help one much. I thought while I was in India that the cave would give me clearer vision. I found it was not so. Then I thought the forest would do so, then, Varanasi. But the same difficulty existed everywhere, because we make our own worlds. If I am evil, the whole world is evil to me.
plain: Moving to a cave, a forest or Varanasi did not bring him clarity, because the same trouble followed him everywhere. We make our own worlds: if I am evil, the whole world looks evil to me.
core_idea: We carry our own world wherever we go

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: I must know the heart of this life, its very essence, what it is, not only how it works and what are its manifestations. I want the why of everything, I leave the how to children.
note: Seeking meaning beyond surface knowledge

tags.when_helps: Someone hungry to understand the deeper why of life, not satisfied with surface explanations.

display_text: I must know the heart of this life, its very essence, what it is, not only how it works and what are its manifestations. I want the why of everything, I leave the how to children.
plain: He wants to know the heart of life itself, what it truly is, not just how it works or what it looks like. He wants the why of everything and leaves the how to children.
core_idea: Seek the why of life, not just how

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter IX. Unity In Diversity
text: A tremendous stream is flowing towards the ocean carrying us all along with it; and though like straws and scraps of paper we may at times float aimlessly about, in the long run we are sure to join the Ocean of Life and Bliss.
note: Feeling aimless; trust in eventual arrival

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling aimless like a straw in a stream, comforted that all lives flow toward something good.

display_text: A tremendous stream is flowing towards the ocean carrying us all along with it; and though like straws and scraps of paper we may at times float aimlessly about, in the long run we are sure to join the Ocean of Life and Bliss.
plain: A huge river is carrying all of us toward the ocean. Though we sometimes drift aimlessly like bits of straw and paper, in the end we will surely reach the Ocean of Life and Bliss.
core_idea: All of us will reach the ocean of bliss

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: The one great idea that to me seems to be clear, and comes out through masses of superstition in every country and in every religion, is the one luminous idea that man is divine, that divinity is our nature.
note: Feeling unworthy; inherent goodness and worth

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels small or unworthy, needing a luminous reminder of the divinity within them.

display_text: The one great idea that to me seems to be clear, and comes out through masses of superstition in every country and in every religion, is the one luminous idea that man is divine, that divinity is our nature.
plain: One bright idea shines through the superstition of every country and religion: human beings are divine, and divinity is our true nature.
core_idea: Human beings are divine by nature

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: The people of old knew that fire lived in the flint and in dry wood, but friction was necessary to call it out. So this fire of freedom and purity is the nature of every soul, and not a quality, because qualities can be acquired and therefore can be lost.
note: Struggle draws out what is already within

tags.when_helps: Someone doubting their spiritual potential, reminded that freedom and purity are their nature, drawn out by effort.

display_text: The people of old knew that fire lived in the flint and in dry wood, but friction was necessary to call it out. So this fire of freedom and purity is the nature of every soul, and not a quality, because qualities can be acquired and therefore can be lost.
plain: Fire lies hidden in flint and dry wood until friction draws it out. In the same way freedom and purity are the very nature of every soul, not qualities, since qualities can be gained and lost.
core_idea: Freedom and purity are the soul's very nature

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: Why should you go to seek for what you never lost? You are pure already, you are free already. If you think you are free, free you are this moment, and if you think you are bound, bound you will be.
note: Feeling trapped; freedom begins in how you see yourself

tags.when_helps: Someone straining to become worthy, who needs to hear they are already pure and free.

display_text: Why should you go to seek for what you never lost? You are pure already, you are free already. If you think you are free, free you are this moment, and if you think you are bound, bound you will be.
plain: Why search for something you never lost, when you are already pure and free? If you think you are free, you are free right now; if you think you are bound, bound you will be.
core_idea: You are free if you think you are

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: As soon as you say, “I am bound,” “I am weak,” “I am helpless,” woe unto you; you rivet one more chain upon yourself. Do not say it, do not think it.
note: Self-defeating talk; feeling helpless

tags.when_helps: Someone repeating 'I am weak, I am helpless' to themselves, who needs a firm push to stop.

display_text: As soon as you say, “I am bound,” “I am weak,” “I am helpless,” woe unto you; you rivet one more chain upon yourself. Do not say it, do not think it.
plain: The moment you say you are bound, weak or helpless, you bring trouble on yourself and add another chain. Do not say it, and do not think it.
core_idea: Calling yourself weak binds you further

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: It is weakness, says the Vedanta, which is the cause of all misery in this world. Weakness is the one cause of suffering. We become miserable because we are weak. We lie, steal, kill, and commit other crimes, because we are weak. We suffer because we are weak. We die because we are weak. Where there is nothing to weaken us, there is no death nor sorrow.
note: Misery and wrongdoing rooted in weakness; seeking strength

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to understand their suffering through the lens of weakness and the need for inner strength.

display_text: It is weakness, says the Vedanta, which is the cause of all misery in this world. Weakness is the one cause of suffering. We become miserable because we are weak. We lie, steal, kill, and commit other crimes, because we are weak. We suffer because we are weak. We die because we are weak. Where there is nothing to weaken us, there is no death nor sorrow.
plain: Vedanta says weakness is the one cause of misery: we lie, steal, kill, suffer and even die because we are weak. Where nothing weakens us, there is neither death nor sorrow.
core_idea: Weakness is the one cause of suffering

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: But however terrible it may seem now, the time will come when we shall look back, each one of us, and smile at every one of those superstitions which covered the pure and eternal soul, and repeat with gladness, with truth, and with strength, I am free, and was free, and always will be free.
note: Fears that will one day seem small

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling bound by present terrors, comforted that one day they will look back and smile.

display_text: But however terrible it may seem now, the time will come when we shall look back, each one of us, and smile at every one of those superstitions which covered the pure and eternal soul, and repeat with gladness, with truth, and with strength, I am free, and was free, and always will be free.
plain: However frightening it seems now, one day we will each look back and smile at the superstitions that hid the pure, eternal soul, and say gladly and truly: I am free, always was and always will be.
core_idea: One day we will know we were always free

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: It is all very well to say, “I am the Pure, the Blessed,” but I cannot show it always in my life. That is true; the ideal is always very hard. Every child that is born sees the sky overhead very far away, but is that any reason why we should not look towards the sky? Would it mend matters to go towards superstition? If we cannot get nectar, would it mend matters for us to drink poison? Would it be any help for us, because we cannot realise the truth immediately, to go into darkness and yield to weakness and superstition?
note: Falling short of ideals; keep aiming high

tags.when_helps: Someone who cannot live up to their ideals and is tempted to give up on them altogether.

display_text: It is all very well to say, “I am the Pure, the Blessed,” but I cannot show it always in my life. That is true; the ideal is always very hard. plain: Living up to the ideal of being pure is hard, but a child still looks up at the distant sky. Failing to reach truth at once is no reason to drink poison by turning to weakness and superstition.
core_idea: A hard ideal is no reason to choose weakness

plain_judge.issue: Compresses the nectar/poison and darkness questions; loses some nuance.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter X. The Freedom Of The Soul
text: Nothing makes us work so well at our best and highest as when all the responsibility is thrown upon ourselves. I challenge everyone of you. How will you behave if I put a little baby in your hands? Your whole life will be changed for the moment; whatever you may be, you must become selfless for the time being. You will give up all your criminal ideas as soon as responsibility is thrown upon you — your whole character will change. So if the whole responsibility is thrown upon our own shoulders, we shall be at our highest and best; when we have nobody to grope towards, no devil to lay our blame upon, no Personal God to carry our burdens, when we are alone responsible, then we shall rise to our highest and best. I am responsible for my fate, I am the bringer of good unto myself, I am the bringer of evil.
note: Taking responsibility; owning one's life without blame

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to blame others or fate, who needs a call to take full responsibility for their life.

display_text: Nothing makes us work so well at our best and highest as when all the responsibility is thrown upon ourselves. I challenge everyone of you.
