plain: We are at our best when all responsibility is ours, as anyone handed a baby turns selfless. With no devil to blame and no personal God to carry our burdens, I alone make my fate, good or bad.
core_idea: Full responsibility brings out our best

plain_judge.issue: Compresses; loses the point that responsibility transforms character.

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Macrocosm
text: Water-drops roll down the mountains into the ocean, and rise again as vapour, go back to the mountains and again come down to the ocean. So, rising and falling, the cycle goes on. So with all lives, so with all existence that we can see, feel, hear, or imagine. Everything that is within the bounds of our knowledge is proceeding in the same way, like breathing in and breathing out in the human body. Everything in creation goes on in this form, one wave rising, another falling, rising again, falling again. Each wave has its hollow, each hollow has its wave.
note: Life's ups and downs; low periods pass

tags.when_helps: Someone in a low point who may find steadiness in the natural rhythm of rising and falling.

display_text: Water-drops roll down the mountains into the ocean, and rise again as vapour, go back to the mountains and again come down to the ocean. So, rising and falling, the cycle goes on. So with all lives, so with all existence that we can see, feel, hear, or imagine. Everything that is within the bounds of our knowledge is proceeding in the same way, like breathing in and breathing out in the human body. Everything in creation goes on in this form, one wave rising, another falling, rising again, falling again. Each wave has its hollow, each hollow has its wave.
plain: Water runs down mountains to the ocean, rises as vapour and returns, over and over. All life and everything we know moves this way, like breathing in and out: each wave has its hollow, each hollow its wave.
core_idea: All existence moves in cycles of rising and falling

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Macrocosm
text: The seed comes out of the tree; it does not immediately become a tree, but has a period of inactivity, or rather, a period of very fine unmanifested action. The seed has to work for some time beneath the soil. It breaks into pieces, degenerates as it were, and regeneration comes out of that degeneration.
note: Fallow periods; breaking down before renewal

tags.when_helps: Someone in a fallow or broken period who might see it as the hidden work before new growth.

display_text: The seed comes out of the tree; it does not immediately become a tree, but has a period of inactivity, or rather, a period of very fine unmanifested action. The seed has to work for some time beneath the soil. It breaks into pieces, degenerates as it were, and regeneration comes out of that degeneration.
plain: A seed does not become a tree at once. It rests and works unseen beneath the soil, breaks apart and seems to decay, and new life grows out of that decay.
core_idea: New life grows out of apparent decay

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Macrocosm
text: “Thou art the man, Thou art the woman, Thou art the strong man walking in the pride of youth, Thou art the old man tottering on crutches, Thou art in everything. Thou art everything, O Lord.”
note: Seeing the divine in everyone, young and old

tags.when_helps: A believer wishing to see the Lord in every person, young and old.

display_text: “Thou art the man, Thou art the woman, Thou art the strong man walking in the pride of youth, Thou art the old man tottering on crutches, Thou art in everything. Thou art everything, O Lord.”
plain: O Lord, you are the man and the woman, the strong youth and the old man on crutches; you are in everything, and you are everything.
core_idea: God is in and is everything

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: Is there nothing permanent in this evanescent human life? Is there nothing, they have asked, which does not die away when this body dies? Is there not something living when this frame crumbles into dust? Is there not something which survives the fire which burns the body into ashes? And if so, what is its destiny? Where does it go? Whence did it come?
note: Facing mortality; asking what survives death

tags.when_helps: Someone asking whether anything survives death, wanting company in that ancient question.

display_text: Is there nothing permanent in this evanescent human life? Is there nothing, they have asked, which does not die away when this body dies? Is there not something living when this frame crumbles into dust? Is there not something which survives the fire which burns the body into ashes? And if so, what is its destiny? Where does it go? Whence did it come?
plain: People have always asked whether anything in this fleeting life is lasting: does something survive when the body dies and burns to ash, and if so, where does it come from and where does it go?
core_idea: Does anything in us survive death?

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: It cannot be that the soul knows, it is knowledge. It cannot be that the soul has existence, but it is existence. It cannot be that the soul is happy, it is happiness itself. That which is happy has borrowed its happiness; that which has knowledge has received its knowledge; and that which has relative existence has only a reflected existence.
note: Happiness as one's true nature, not borrowed

tags.when_helps: A reflective seeker exploring the idea that the soul is itself knowledge, existence and happiness.

display_text: It cannot be that the soul knows, it is knowledge. It cannot be that the soul has existence, but it is existence. It cannot be that the soul is happy, it is happiness itself. That which is happy has borrowed its happiness; that which has knowledge has received its knowledge; and that which has relative existence has only a reflected existence.
plain: The soul does not have knowledge, existence or happiness; it is knowledge, existence and happiness itself. Anything that merely has these has borrowed them and reflects them.
core_idea: The soul is knowledge, existence and happiness itself

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: Neither you, nor I nor anyone present, has come out of zero, nor will go back to zero. We have been existing eternally, and will exist, and there is no power under the sun or above the sun which can undo your or my existence or send us back to zero.
note: Fear of death or annihilation; enduring existence

tags.when_helps: Someone frightened of annihilation, comforted by the claim that their existence cannot be undone.

display_text: Neither you, nor I nor anyone present, has come out of zero, nor will go back to zero. We have been existing eternally, and will exist, and there is no power under the sun or above the sun which can undo your or my existence or send us back to zero.

core_idea: We have always existed and always will

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: A child begins to play on the piano. At first she must pay attention to every key she is fingering, and as she goes on and on for months and years, the playing becomes almost involuntary, instinctive. What was first done with conscious will does not require later on an effort of the will.
note: Learning a skill; effort becomes ease with practice

tags.when_helps: Someone frustrated that a new habit or skill still takes effort, reassured that practice makes it natural.

plain: A child learning piano must first watch every key, but after months and years the playing becomes almost automatic. What first took conscious effort later needs no effort of will.
core_idea: Practice turns conscious effort into instinct

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: We do not look at our own faults; the eyes do not see themselves, they see the eyes of everybody else. We human beings are very slow to recognise our own weakness, our own faults, so long as we can lay the blame upon somebody else. Men in general lay all the blame of life on their fellow-men, or, failing that, on God, or they conjure up a ghost, and say it is fate. Where is fate, and who is fate? We reap what we sow. We are the makers of our own fate. None else has the blame, none has the praise.
note: Blaming others or fate; owning one's choices

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone quick to blame others or fate, ready to look honestly at their own part.

plain: Like eyes that see others but not themselves, we miss our own faults and blame people, God or fate. But we reap what we sow: we make our own fate, and no one else earns blame or praise.

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: The wind is blowing; those vessels whose sails are unfurled catch it, and go forward on their way, but those which have their sails furled do not catch the wind. Is that the fault of the wind? Is it the fault of the merciful Father, whose wind of mercy is blowing without ceasing, day and night, whose mercy knows no decay, is it His fault that some of us are happy and some unhappy? We make our own destiny. His sun shines for the weak as well as for the strong. His wind blows for saint and sinner alike.
note: Feeling unlucky; openness to grace and opportunity

tags.when_helps: A believer who resents God for their unhappiness, invited to open their own sails to grace.

display_text: The wind is blowing; those vessels whose sails are unfurled catch it, and go forward on their way, but those which have their sails furled do not catch the wind. plain: The wind fills only ships with sails raised; God's mercy blows day and night for saint and sinner alike, so it is not His fault that some are happy and some not. We make our own destiny.
core_idea: God's mercy is for all; we make our destiny

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: His infinite mercy is open to every one, at all times, in all places, under all conditions, unfailing, unswerving. Upon us depends how we use it. Upon us depends how we utilise it. tags.when_helps: Someone stuck in blaming others or God who is ready to take ownership and try to do better.

display_text: His infinite mercy is open to every one, at all times, in all places, under all conditions, unfailing, unswerving. Upon us depends how we use it. Upon us depends how we utilise it. display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm
text: Say, “This misery that I am suffering is of my own doing, and that very thing proves that it will have to be undone by me alone.” That which I created, I can demolish; that which is created by some one else I shall never be able to destroy. All the strength and succour you want is within yourselves.

display: Jnana-Yoga: The Microcosm

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XII. Immortality
text: Often in the turmoil and struggle of our lives we seem to forget it, but suddenly some one dies — one, perhaps, whom we loved, one near and dear to our hearts is snatched away from us — and the struggle, the din and turmoil of the world around us, cease for a moment, and the soul asks the old questions “What after this?” “What becomes of the soul?”
note: Grief after losing a loved one

tags.when_helps: Someone recently bereaved, suddenly asking what becomes of the soul, who needs to know this question is shared.

display_text: Often in the turmoil and struggle of our lives we seem to forget it, but suddenly some one dies — one, perhaps, whom we loved, one near and dear to our hearts is snatched away from us — and the struggle, the din and turmoil of the world around us, cease for a moment, and the soul asks the old questions “What after this?” “What becomes of the soul?”

core_idea: A loved one's death stirs questions about the soul

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XII. Immortality
text: There is no motion in a straight line. Everything moves in a circle; a straight line, infinitely produced, becomes a circle. If that is the case, there cannot be eternal degeneration for any soul. It cannot be. Everything must complete the circle, and come back to its source.
note: Feeling lost or fallen; no one is beyond return

tags.when_helps: Someone who fears they or another are lost forever, comforted that every soul returns to its source.

display_text: There is no motion in a straight line. Everything moves in a circle; a straight line, infinitely produced, becomes a circle. If that is the case, there cannot be eternal degeneration for any soul. It cannot be. Everything must complete the circle, and come back to its source.
plain: Nothing moves in a straight line; everything moves in a circle. So no soul can go downhill forever: everything must complete the circle and return to its source.
core_idea: Every soul must return to its source

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XII. Immortality
text: Sometimes you see a cloud moving before the moon, and you think that the moon is moving. When you are in a train you think the land is flying, or when you are in a boat, you think the water moves. In reality you are neither going nor coming, you are not being born, nor going to be reborn; you are infinite, ever-present, beyond all causation, and ever-free.
note: Fear of death; the unchanging self beneath change

tags.when_helps: Someone anxious about birth, death and change, who might find stillness in seeing their true self as unmoving.

display_text: Sometimes you see a cloud moving before the moon, and you think that the moon is moving. plain: A cloud passing the moon makes the moon seem to move, and from a train the land seems to fly. Likewise you are not really coming or going, born or reborn; you are infinite, ever-present, beyond cause and ever free.
core_idea: You are not born or reborn; you are infinite

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XII. Immortality
text: Wherever there are two, there is fear, there is danger, there is conflict, there is strife. When it is all One, who is there to hate, who is there to struggle with? When it is all He, with whom can you fight?

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XII. Immortality
text: What makes you weak? What makes you fear? You are the One Being in the universe. What frightens you? Stand up then and be free. display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XII. Immortality
text: What can frighten you? If the suns come down, and the moons crumble into dust, and systems after systems are hurled into annihilation, what is that to you? Stand as a rock; you are indestructible.

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: We see in this life that we can shape and form our future every one of us, every day, is trying to shape the morrow; today we fix the fate of the morrow; tomorrow we shall fix the fate of the day after, and so on.

core_idea: Each day we shape the next

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: This “me and mine” is the very root of all the evil in the world. If you ask a dualist, “Is your child yours?” he will say, “It is God’s. My property is not mine, it is God’s.” Everything should be held as God’s.
note: Possessiveness and attachment to what we own

tags.when_helps: Someone clinging possessively to people or things, invited to hold them as belonging to God.

display_text: This “me and mine” is the very root of all the evil in the world. If you ask a dualist, “Is your child yours?” he will say, “It is God’s. My property is not mine, it is God’s.” Everything should be held as God’s.
plain: The sense of me and mine is the root of all evil in the world. A dualist says his child and property belong not to him but to God, and everything should be held that way.
core_idea: Me and mine is the root of evil

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: God is the centre of attraction for every soul, and the dualist says, “A needle covered up with clay will not be attracted by a magnet, but as soon as the clay is washed off, it will be attracted.” God is the magnet and human soul is the needle, and its evil works, the dirt and dust that cover it.
note: Feeling far from God; purifying the heart

tags.when_helps: A believer feeling far from God because of past wrongs, reminded the pull remains once the dust is washed off.

display_text: God is the centre of attraction for every soul, and the dualist says, “A needle covered up with clay will not be attracted by a magnet, but as soon as the clay is washed off, it will be attracted.” God is the magnet and human soul is the needle, and its evil works, the dirt and dust that cover it.
plain: God draws every soul as a magnet draws a needle. The dualist says a needle caked in clay will not move toward the magnet until the clay is washed off; the soul's evil deeds are that dirt.
core_idea: Evil deeds cover the soul's pull toward God

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: We have made ourselves so weak; we have made ourselves so low. We may make great claims, but naturally we want to lean on somebody else. We are like little, weak plants, always wanting a support. How many times I have been asked for a “comfortable religion!” Very few men ask for the truth, fewer still dare to learn the truth, and fewest of all dare to follow it in all its practical bearings.
note: Seeking comfort over truth; courage to follow it

tags.when_helps: Someone looking for easy comfort who is ready to be challenged to seek and follow the truth.

display_text: We have made ourselves so weak; we have made ourselves so low. We may make great claims, but naturally we want to lean on somebody else. We are like little, weak plants, always wanting a support. How many times I have been asked for a “comfortable religion!” Very few men ask for the truth, fewer still dare to learn the truth, and fewest of all dare to follow it in all its practical bearings.
plain: We have made ourselves weak, always wanting something to lean on like small plants needing a stake. Many want a comfortable religion; very few ask for truth, fewer dare to learn it, and fewest dare to live it.
core_idea: Few dare to seek and live the truth

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: Sometimes a sick man lying on his bed may hear a tap on the door. He gets up and opens it and finds no one there. He goes back to bed, and again he hears a tap. He gets up and opens the door. Nobody is there. At last he finds that it was his own heartbeat which he fancied was a knock at the door. Thus man, after this vain search after various gods outside himself, completes the circle, and comes back to the point from which he started — the human soul, and he finds that the God whom he was searching in hill and dale, whom he was seeking in every brook, in every temple, in churches and heavens, that God whom he was even imagining as sitting in heaven and ruling the world, is his own Self.
note: Searching outside for what lies within

tags.when_helps: A weary seeker who has looked for God everywhere outside, ready to look within.

display_text: Sometimes a sick man lying on his bed may hear a tap on the door. He gets up and opens it and finds no one there. He goes back to bed, and again he hears a tap. plain: A sick man keeps answering a knock and finding no one, until he realises it was his own heartbeat. So, after seeking God in temples, rivers and heavens, a person finds God is his own Self.
core_idea: The God we seek outside is our own Self

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: You are never in illusion; it is illusion that is in you, before you. A cloud is here; another comes and pushes it aside and takes its place. Still another comes and pushes that one away. As before the eternal blue sky, clouds of various hue and colour come, remain for a short time and disappear, leaving it the same eternal blue, even so are you, eternally pure, eternally perfect.
note: Passing troubles like clouds; your true self stays untouched

tags.when_helps: Someone caught up in shifting moods who may find steadiness in seeing them as clouds before a clear sky.

display_text: You are never in illusion; it is illusion that is in you, before you. A cloud is here; another comes and pushes it aside and takes its place. Still another comes and pushes that one away. As before the eternal blue sky, clouds of various hue and colour come, remain for a short time and disappear, leaving it the same eternal blue, even so are you, eternally pure, eternally perfect.
plain: You are never inside illusion; illusion passes before you. As clouds of every colour come and go across the blue sky and leave it unchanged, you remain forever pure and perfect.
core_idea: Like the sky, you stay pure as illusions pass

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: When man has seen himself as one with the Infinite Being of the universe, when all separateness has ceased, when all men and women, an gods and angels, all animals and plants, and the whole universe have melted into that Oneness, then all fear disappears. Can I hurt myself? Can I kill myself? Can I injure myself? Whom to fear? Can you fear yourself? Then will all sorrow disappear. What can cause me sorrow? I am the One Existence of the universe. Then all jealousies will disappear; of whom to be jealous? Of myself? Then all bad feelings disappear. Against whom can I have bad feeling? Against myself? There is none in the universe but I.
note: Oneness dissolving fear, sorrow and jealousy

tags.when_helps: A seeker beset by fear, jealousy or ill will who is drawn to oneness as their dissolution.

display_text: When man has seen himself as one with the Infinite Being of the universe, when all separateness has ceased, when all men and women, all gods and angels, all animals and plants, and the whole universe have melted into that Oneness, then all fear disappears. plain: When a person sees himself as one with the Infinite and all separateness melts away, fear, sorrow, jealousy and ill will vanish. Who is left to fear or resent, when there is no one in the universe but I?
core_idea: In oneness, fear, sorrow and jealousy vanish

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIII. The Atman
text: Injure none, deny the position of none; take man where he stands and, if you can, lend him a helping hand and put him on a higher platform, but do not injure and do not destroy. All will come to truth in the long run.
note: Meeting others where they are; helping without harming

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to tear down another's views, reminded to meet people where they stand and help.

display_text: Injure none, deny the position of none; take man where he stands and, if you can, lend him a helping hand and put him on a higher platform, but do not injure and do not destroy. All will come to truth in the long run.
plain: Harm no one and dismiss no one's view; meet people where they are and, if you can, help them higher, but never hurt or tear down. Everyone will reach truth in the end.
core_idea: Meet people where they are; harm no one

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIV. The Atman: Its Bondage And Freedom
text: Each work we do, each thought we think, produces an impression, called in Sanskrit Samskâra, upon the mind and the sum total of these impressions becomes the tremendous force which is called “character”. The character of a man is what he has created for himself; it is the result of the mental and physical actions that he has done in his life.
note: Habits and actions shape who we become

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to change who they are, seeing how each thought and act builds character.

display_text: Each work we do, each thought we think, produces an impression, called in Sanskrit Samskâra, upon the mind and the sum total of these impressions becomes the tremendous force which is called “character”. The character of a man is what he has created for himself; it is the result of the mental and physical actions that he has done in his life.
plain: Every act and thought leaves an impression on the mind, called samskara in Sanskrit, and all these together form the powerful force we call character. Your character is what you have made of yourself through your actions.
core_idea: Character is built from every act and thought

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XIV. The Atman: Its Bondage And Freedom
text: Like the caterpillar that takes the thread from its own mouth and builds its cocoon and at last finds itself caught inside the cocoon, we have bound ourselves by our own actions, we have thrown the network of our actions around ourselves. We have set the law of causation in motion, and we find it hard to get ourselves out of it. We have set the wheel in motion, and we are being crushed under it.
note: Feeling trapped by consequences of one's own choices

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone feeling trapped by consequences of their own choices, wanting to understand how they got caught.

display_text: Like the caterpillar that takes the thread from its own mouth and builds its cocoon and at last finds itself caught inside the cocoon, we have bound ourselves by our own actions, we have thrown the network of our actions around ourselves. We have set the law of causation in motion, and we find it hard to get ourselves out of it. We have set the wheel in motion, and we are being crushed under it.
plain: Like a caterpillar trapped in the cocoon it spun from its own thread, we have tied ourselves up in our own actions. We set the wheel of cause and effect turning, and now it crushes us.
core_idea: We are trapped by our own actions

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: This mind is like a lake, and every thought is like a wave upon that lake. Just as in the lake waves rise and then fall down and disappear, so these thought-waves are continually rising in the mind-stuff and then disappearing, but they do not disappear for ever. They become finer and finer, but they are all there, ready to start up at another time when called upon to do so.
note: Thoughts that pass but resurface; understanding the restless mind

tags.when_helps: Someone troubled by recurring thoughts who wants a clear image of how the mind works.

display_text: This mind is like a lake, and every thought is like a wave upon that lake. Just as in the lake waves rise and then fall down and disappear, so these thought-waves are continually rising in the mind-stuff and then disappearing, but they do not disappear for ever. They become finer and finer, but they are all there, ready to start up at another time when called upon to do so.
plain: The mind is like a lake and each thought a wave on it. Thought-waves rise and seem to vanish, but they never disappear completely; they become subtler and wait, ready to rise again when called.
core_idea: Thoughts never vanish; they wait to rise again

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: To the vast majority of men nature appears to be only a changing, whirling, combining, mingling mass of change. Few of us ever have a glimpse of the calm sea behind. For us it is always lashed into waves; this universe appears to us only as a tossing mass of waves.
note: Caught in constant change; glimpsing calm beneath turmoil

tags.when_helps: Someone lost in the churn of change who longs for a glimpse of the calm beneath it.

display_text: To the vast majority of men nature appears to be only a changing, whirling, combining, mingling mass of change. Few of us ever have a glimpse of the calm sea behind. For us it is always lashed into waves; this universe appears to us only as a tossing mass of waves.
plain: To most people nature looks like nothing but a whirling, shifting mass of change. Few ever glimpse the calm sea underneath; to us the universe seems only tossing waves.
core_idea: Few glimpse the calm beneath constant change

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: Look at the waves in the sea. Not one wave is really different from the sea, but what makes the wave apparently different? Name and form; the form of the wave and the name which we give to it, “wave”. This is what makes it different from the sea. When name and form go, it is the same sea. Who can make any real difference between the wave and the sea?
note: Separateness and belonging; individual as part of the whole

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling separate who is drawn to the image of a wave that is never apart from the sea.

display_text: Look at the waves in the sea. Not one wave is really different from the sea, but what makes the wave apparently different? Name and form; the form of the wave and the name which we give to it, “wave”. This is what makes it different from the sea. When name and form go, it is the same sea. Who can make any real difference between the wave and the sea?
plain: A wave is not truly different from the sea; only its shape and the name we give it set it apart. Take away name and form, and it is the same sea.
core_idea: Only name and form separate wave from sea

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: I am studying a book, page after page is being read and turned over. Another page comes and is turned over. Who changes? Who comes and goes? Not I, but the book. This whole nature is a book before the soul, chapter after chapter is being read and turned over, and every now and then a scene opens. That is read and turned over. A fresh one comes, but the soul is ever the same — eternal. It is nature that is changing, not the soul of man. This never changes. Birth and death are in nature, not in you.
note: Facing death and change; the self that stays constant

tags.when_helps: Someone unsettled by life's changing chapters, steadied by the idea that the witness within stays the same.

display_text: I am studying a book, page after page is being read and turned over. Another page comes and is turned over. Who changes? Who comes and goes? Not I, but the book. This whole nature is a book before the soul, chapter after chapter is being read and turned over, and every now and then a scene opens. That is read and turned over. A fresh one comes, but the soul is ever the same — eternal. It is nature that is changing, not the soul of man. This never changes. Birth and death are in nature, not in you.
plain: When I read a book, the pages turn, not I; nature is such a book before the soul, scene after scene, while the soul stays the same forever. Birth and death belong to nature, not to you.
core_idea: Nature changes; the soul stays the same

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: The worst lie that you ever tell yourself is that you were born a sinner or a wicked man. He alone is a sinner who sees a sinner in another man.
note: Guilt, self-condemnation and judging others

tags.when_helps: Someone who believes they are inherently bad, needing to hear that is the worst lie they tell themselves.

display_text: The worst lie that you ever tell yourself is that you were born a sinner or a wicked man. He alone is a sinner who sees a sinner in another man.
plain: The worst lie you can tell yourself is that you were born a sinner or wicked. Only the person who sees a sinner in someone else is a sinner.
core_idea: Only one who sees sinners is a sinner

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: Once in Western India I was travelling in the desert country on the coast of the Indian Ocean. For days and days I used to travel on foot through the desert, but it was to my surprise that I saw every day beautiful lakes, with trees all round them, and the shadows of the trees upside down and vibrating there. “How wonderful it looks and they call this a desert country!” I said to myself. Nearly a month I travelled, seeing these wonderful lakes and trees and plants. One day I was very thirsty and wanted to have a drink of water, so I started to go to one of these clear, beautiful lakes, and as I approached, it vanished. And with a flash it came to my brain, “This is the mirage about which I have read all my life,” and with that came also the idea that throughout the whole of this month, every day, I had been seeing the mirage and did not know it. The next morning I began my march. There was again the lake, but with it came also the idea that it was the mirage and not a true lake. So is it with this universe. We are all travelling in this mirage of the world day after day, month after month, year after year, not knowing that it is a mirage.
note: Disillusionment; seeing through what we chased

situations: loss of a dream or plan
tags.when_helps: Someone whose hoped-for thing vanished on approach, reflecting on how much of what we chase is mirage.

core_idea: The world is a mirage we do not recognise

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: There is, you must remember, all the difference of pole to pole between realisation and mere talking. Any fool can talk. Even parrots talk. Talking is one thing, and realising is another. Philosophies, and doctrines, and arguments, and books, and theories, and churches, and sects, and all these things are good in their own way; but when that realisation comes, these things drop away. For instance, maps are good, but when you see the country itself, and look again at the maps, what a great difference you find!
note: Living experience versus talk and theory

tags.when_helps: Someone well-read in spiritual ideas but feeling unchanged, reminded that realisation differs from talk.

display_text: There is, you must remember, all the difference of pole to pole between realisation and mere talking. Any fool can talk. Even parrots talk. Talking is one thing, and realising is another. Philosophies, and doctrines, and arguments, and books, and theories, and churches, and sects, and all these things are good in their own way; but when that realisation comes, these things drop away. For instance, maps are good, but when you see the country itself, and look again at the maps, what a great difference you find!
plain: Realising truth and merely talking about it are worlds apart; anyone can talk, even parrots. Philosophies, books and churches help in their way, but they fall away once realisation comes, as maps do when you see the country itself.
core_idea: Talking about truth is not realising it

display: Jnana-Yoga: Chapter XV. The Real And The Apparent Man
text: How can you see evil until there is evil in you? How can you see the thief, unless he is there, sitting in the heart of your heart? How can you see the murderer until you are yourself the murderer? Be good, and evil will vanish for you.
note: Judging others; what we see reflects ourselves

tags.when_helps: Someone consumed by seeing evil in others who is ready to look at what that reveals in themselves.

display_text: How can you see evil until there is evil in you? How can you see the thief, unless he is there, sitting in the heart of your heart? How can you see the murderer until you are yourself the murderer? Be good, and evil will vanish for you.
plain: How can you see evil, a thief or a murderer, unless it is already sitting in your own heart? Be good, and evil will disappear for you.
core_idea: Be good and evil disappears for you

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Definition Of Bhakti
text: Bhakti-Yoga is a real, genuine search after the Lord, a search beginning, continuing, and ending in love. One single moment of the madness of extreme love to God brings us eternal freedom.
note: Spiritual seeking through love and devotion

tags.when_helps: A devotee longing for God who wants to hear that love itself is the path.

display_text: Bhakti-Yoga is a real, genuine search after the Lord, a search beginning, continuing, and ending in love. One single moment of the madness of extreme love to God brings us eternal freedom.
plain: Bhakti-Yoga is a sincere search for the Lord that begins, goes on and ends in love. A single moment of wildly intense love for God brings eternal freedom.
core_idea: One moment of intense love for God frees us

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Definition Of Bhakti
text: All the weak and undeveloped minds in every religion or country have only one way of loving their own ideal, i.e. by hating every other ideal.
note: Intolerance; loving one's own by hating others

tags.when_helps: Someone troubled by religious intolerance, or tempted toward it, who needs a plain word against it.

display_text: All the weak and undeveloped minds in every religion or country have only one way of loving their own ideal, i.e. by hating every other ideal.
plain: In every religion and country, weak and immature minds can love their own ideal only by hating every other one.
core_idea: Weak minds love their ideal by hating others

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Definition Of Bhakti
text: Three things are necessary for a bird to fly — the two wings and the tail as a rudder for steering. Jnana (Knowledge) is the one wing, Bhakti (Love) is the other, and Yoga is the tail that keeps up the balance.
note: Balancing head, heart and practice in life

tags.when_helps: A seeker unsure whether to follow knowledge or devotion, shown how both work together with practice.

display_text: Three things are necessary for a bird to fly — the two wings and the tail as a rudder for steering. Jnana (Knowledge) is the one wing, Bhakti (Love) is the other, and Yoga is the tail that keeps up the balance.
plain: A bird needs two wings and a tail to fly. Knowledge is one wing, love of God the other, and yoga is the tail that keeps the balance.
core_idea: Knowledge, love and yoga must work together

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Definition Of Bhakti
text: That deathless love which the ignorant have for the fleeting objects of the senses — as I keep meditating on Thee — may not that love slip away from my heart!
note: Prayer to keep devotion as strong as desire

tags.when_helps: A devotee who wants their love for God to burn as strongly as worldly attachments do.

display_text: That deathless love which the ignorant have for the fleeting objects of the senses — as I keep meditating on Thee — may not that love slip away from my heart!
plain: A prayer: as I keep meditating on You, may I never lose the same unfailing love that ignorant people feel for passing pleasures of the senses.
core_idea: Love God as fiercely as others love pleasure

plain_judge.issue: Wording is ambiguous: could read as wanting love of sense objects rather than that intensity turned to God.

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter III. Spiritual Realisation, The Aim Of Bhakti-Yoga
text: One ounce of the practice of righteousness and of spiritual Self-realisation outweighs tons and tons of frothy talk and nonsensical sentiments.
note: Practice over talk; living what you believe

tags.when_helps: Someone tired of endless spiritual talk who needs a reminder that a little practice outweighs much discussion.

display_text: One ounce of the practice of righteousness and of spiritual Self-realisation outweighs tons and tons of frothy talk and nonsensical sentiments.
plain: A little practice of right living and spiritual self-realisation is worth more than tons of empty talk and silly sentiment.
core_idea: A little practice outweighs much empty talk

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter IV. The Need Of Guru
text: Every soul is destined to be perfect, and every being, in the end, will attain the state of perfection. Whatever we are now is the result of our acts and thoughts in the past; and whatever we shall be in the future will be the result of what we think end do now. But this, the shaping of our own destinies, does not preclude our receiving help from outside; nay, in the vast majority of cases such help is absolutely necessary. When it comes, the higher powers and possibilities of the soul are quickened, spiritual life is awakened, growth is animated, and man becomes holy and perfect in the end.
note: Shaping your future; accepting help from others

tags.when_helps: Someone shaping their own growth who wonders whether it is all right to seek outside help too.

display_text: Every soul is destined to be perfect, and every being, in the end, will attain the state of perfection. Whatever we are now is the result of our acts and thoughts in the past; and whatever we shall be in the future will be the result of what we think and do now. But this, the shaping of our own destinies, does not preclude our receiving help from outside; nay, in the vast majority of cases such help is absolutely necessary. When it comes, the higher powers and possibilities of the soul are quickened, spiritual life is awakened, growth is animated, and man becomes holy and perfect in the end.
plain: Every soul will be perfect in the end; what we are comes from past thoughts and acts, and what we will be from what we do now. Yet we mostly need outside help to awaken the soul's higher powers.
core_idea: We shape our destiny, but need outside help

plain_judge.issue: Softens 'absolutely necessary' help to 'mostly need'; drops becoming holy and perfect.

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter IV. The Need Of Guru
text: We may study books all our lives, we may become very intellectual, but in the end we find that we have not developed at all spiritually. It is not true that a high order of intellectual development always goes hand in hand with a proportionate development of the spiritual side in Man.
note: Knowledge without inner growth; learning versus living

tags.when_helps: Someone well-read but spiritually unchanged, ready to see that intellect alone is not growth.

display_text: We may study books all our lives, we may become very intellectual, but in the end we find that we have not developed at all spiritually. It is not true that a high order of intellectual development always goes hand in hand with a proportionate development of the spiritual side in Man.
plain: We can study books our whole lives and become very clever, yet find we have not grown spiritually at all. Great intellect does not always bring equal spiritual growth.
core_idea: Intellect does not bring spiritual growth

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter IV. The Need Of Guru
text: Many a time in our lives, somebody dies whom we loved; we receive a blow; we feel that the world is slipping between our fingers, that we want something surer and higher, and that we must become religious. In a few days that wave of feeling has passed away, and we are left stranded just where we were before.
note: Loss stirring a search for meaning that fades

tags.when_helps: Someone whose loss stirred a spiritual turn that is now fading, wanting to understand that pattern.

display_text: Many a time in our lives, somebody dies whom we loved; we receive a blow; we feel that the world is slipping between our fingers, that we want something surer and higher, and that we must become religious. In a few days that wave of feeling has passed away, and we are left stranded just where we were before.
plain: Often when someone we love dies, we feel the world slipping away and resolve to seek something higher and become religious. In a few days the feeling passes, and we are left just where we were.
core_idea: Grief's urge toward religion soon fades

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter V. Qualifications Of The Aspirant And The Teacher
text: To pant for religion truly is a very difficult thing, not at all so easy as we generally imagine. Hearing religious talks or reading religious books is no proof yet of a real want felt in the heart; there must be a continuous struggle, a constant fight, an unremitting grappling with our lower nature, till the higher want is actually felt and the victory is achieved. It is not a question of one or two days, of years, or of lives; the struggle may have to go on for hundreds of lifetimes. The success sometimes may come immediately, but we must be ready to wait patiently even for what may look like an infinite length of time. The student who sets out with such a spirit of perseverance will surely find success and realisation at last.
note: Patience and perseverance on a long inner path

tags.when_helps: A seeker discouraged by slow progress who needs to hear perseverance will bring realisation in time.

plain: Truly longing for religion is hard; talks and books do not prove it, only a constant fight with your lower nature until the longing is real. It may take many lifetimes, but whoever perseveres will succeed.

text: Bhagavân Ramakrishna used to tell a story of some men who went into a mango orchard and busied themselves in counting the leaves, the twigs, and the branches, examining their colour, comparing their size, and noting down everything most carefully, and then got up a learned discussion on each of these topics, which were undoubtedly highly interesting to them. But one of them, more sensible than the others, did not care for all these things. and instead thereof, began to eat the mango fruit. And was he not wise?

text: Religion, which is the highest knowledge and the highest wisdom, cannot be bought, nor can it be acquired from books. display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter IX. The Chosen Ideal
text: Very few indeed are those who are at once the possessors of an extensive sympathy and power of appreciation, as well as an intensity of love. We find, as a rule, that liberal and sympathetic sects lose the intensity of religious feeling, and in their hands, religion is apt to degenerate into a kind of politico-social club life. On the other hand, intensely narrow sectaries, whilst displaying a very commendable love of their own ideals, are seen to have acquired every particle of that love by hating every one who is not of exactly the same opinions as themselves. Would to God that this world was full of men who were as intense in their love as worldwide in their sympathies! But such are only few and far between.
note: Holding deep conviction without hating those who differ

tags.when_helps: Someone torn between deep conviction and openness to others, hoping to hold both.

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter IX. The Chosen Ideal
text: The tender plant of spirituality will die if exposed too early to the action of a constant change of ideas and ideals. Many people, in the name of what may be called religious liberalism, may be seen feeding their idle curiosity with a continuous succession of different ideals. With them, hearing new things grows into a kind of disease, a sort of religious drink-mania. They want to hear new things just by way of getting a temporary nervous excitement, and when one such exciting influence has had its effect on them, they are ready for another. Religion is with these people a sort of intellectual opium-eating, and there it ends.
note: Restlessly chasing new ideas instead of committing to a path

tags.when_helps: Someone hopping from one teaching to the next for excitement who needs to commit to one path.

display: Bhakti-Yoga: Chapter X. The Method And The Means
text: It is better to have internal purity alone when minute attention to external observances is not practicable. But woe unto the man and woe unto the nation that forgets the real, internal, spiritual essentials of religion and mechanically clutches with death-like grasp at all external forms and never lets them go. The forms have value only so far as they are expressions of the life within. If they have ceased to express life, crush them out without mercy.

display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter II. The Bhakta’s Renunciation Results From Love
text: It is the same feeling of love, well or ill directed, that impels one man to do good and to give all he has to the poor, while it makes another man cut the throats of his brethren and take away all their possessions. The former loves others as much as the latter loves himself. The direction of the love is bad in the case of the latter, but it is right and proper in the other case. The same fire that cooks a meal for us may burn a child, and it is no fault of the fire if it does so; the difference lies in the way in which it is used.

display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter II. The Bhakta’s Renunciation Results From Love
text: Take yourself away from all the world’s little selfish clingings. Do not look upon humanity as the centre of all your human and higher interests. Stand as a witness, as a student, and observe the phenomena of nature. Have the feeling of personal non-attachment with regard to man, and see how this mighty feeling of love is working itself out in the world. Sometimes a little friction is produced, but that is only in the course of the struggle to attain the higher real love. Sometimes there is a little fight or a little fall; but it is all only by the way. Stand aside, and freely let these frictions come. You feel the frictions only when you are in the current of the world, but when you are outside of it simply as a witness and as a student, you will be able to see that there are millions and millions of channels in which God is manifesting Himself as Love.

display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter III. The Naturalness Of Bhakti-Yoga And Its Central Secret
text: We find that pleasures and pains are very common and oftrecurring feelings in our lives. When a man feels pain because he has not wealth or some such worldly thing, he is giving a wrong direction to the feeling. Still pain has its uses. Let a man feel pain that he has not reached the Highest, that he has not reached God, and that pain will be to his salvation. When you become glad that you have a handful of coins, it is a wrong direction given to the faculty of joy; it should be given a higher direction, it must be made to serve the Highest Ideal. Pleasure in that kind of ideal must surely be our highest joy. This same thing is true of all our other feelings.
note: Redirecting pain and pleasure toward higher aims

text: With the love of God will come, as a sure effect, the love of every one in the universe. The nearer we approach God, the more do we begin to see that all things are in Him. display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter V. Universal Love And How It Leads To Self-Surrender
text: As a result of this kind of intense all-absorbing love, comes the feeling of perfect self-surrender, the conviction that nothing that happens is against us, Aprâtikulya. Then the loving soul is able to say, if pain comes, “Welcome pain.” If misery comes, it will say, “Welcome misery, you are also from the Beloved.” If a serpent comes, it will say, “Welcome serpent.” If death comes, such a Bhakta will welcome it with a smile. “Blessed am I that they all come to me; they are all welcome.” The Bhakta in this state of perfect resignation, arising out of intense love to God and to all that are His, ceases to distinguish between pleasure and pain in so far as they affect him. He does not know what it is to complain of pain or misery; and this kind of uncomplaining resignation to the will of God, who is all love, is indeed a worthier acquisition than all the glory of grand and heroic performances.
note: Accepting whatever comes, pain included, without complaint

tags.when_helps: A devout reader at peace seeking deeper surrender to God's will in pain and pleasure alike.

display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter V. Universal Love And How It Leads To Self-Surrender
text: Ordinarily human love is seen to flourish only in places where it is returned; where love is not returned for love, cold indifference is the natural result. There are, however, rare instances in which we may notice love exhibiting itself even where there is no return of love. We may compare this kind of love, far purposes of illustration, to the love of the moth for the fire; the insect loves the fire, falls into it, and dies. It is indeed in the nature of this insect to love so. To love because it is the nature of love to love is undeniably the highest and the most unselfish manifestation of love that may be seen in the world.
note: Loving without needing love returned

tags.safety_reason: Praises the moth that falls into the fire and dies as the highest form of unrequited love.
tags.when_helps: A settled reader reflecting on what it means to love without expecting love in return.

Those who worship God because they wish Him to bestow favours on them are sure not to worship Him if those favours are not forthcoming.
plain: Where something is wanted in return, there is no real love, only shopkeeping. While we expect favours from God for our worship, true love cannot grow; those who worship for favours will stop when the favours do not come.
core_idea: Love that seeks a reward is shopkeeping

display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter VII. The Triangle Of Love
text: Begging is not the language of love. To worship God even for the sake of salvation or any other rewards equally degenerate. Love knows no reward. Love is always for love’s sake. The Bhakta loves because he cannot help loving. When you see a beautiful scenery and fall in love with it, you do not demand anything in the way of favour from the scenery, nor does the scenery demand anything from you. Yet the vision thereof brings you to a blissful state of the mind; it tones down all the friction in your soul, it makes you calm, almost raises you, for the time being, beyond your mortal nature and places you in a condition of quite divine ecstasy.
note: Love for its own sake, asking nothing back

tags.when_helps: Someone moved by beauty or love who wants to understand love that seeks nothing in return.

display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter VII. The Triangle Of Love
text: So long as there is any fear in the heart, how can there be love also? Love conquers naturally all fear. Think of a young mother in the street and a dog barking at her; she is frightened and flies into nearest house. But suppose the next day she is in the street with her child, and a lion springs upon the child. Where will be her position now? Of course, in the very mouth of the lion, protecting her child. Love conquers all fear. Fear comes from the selfish idea of cutting one’s self off from the universe. The smaller and the more selfish I make myself, the more is my fear. If a man thinks he is a little nothing, fear will surely come upon him. And the less you think of yourself as an insignificant person, the less fear there will be for you.
note: Fear, smallness, and how love overcomes fear

tags.when_helps: Someone gripped by fear who could find courage in how love overcomes it, as a mother protects her child.

display: Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion: Chapter IX. Human Representations Of The Divine Ideal Of Love
text: The world is just a playground, and we are here having good fun, having a game; and God is with us playing all the while, and we are with Him playing. God is our eternal playmate. How beautifully He is playing! The play is finished when the cycle: comes to an end. There is rest for a shorter or longer time; again all come out and play. It is only when you forget that it is all play and that you are also helping in the play, it is only then that misery and sorrows come. Then the heart becomes heavy, then the world weighs upon you with tremendous power. But as soon as you give up the serious idea of reality as the characteristic of the changing incidents of the three minutes of life and know it to be but a stage on which we are playing, helping Him to play, at once misery ceases for you.
note: Taking life less heavily; seeing it as play

tags.when_helps: Someone weighed down, taking life's troubles with crushing seriousness, who might find relief in seeing life as play shared with God.

text: Inactivity, as we understand it in the sense of passivity, certainly cannot be the goal. Were it so, then the walls around us would be the most intelligent; they are inactive. text: Man never progresses from error to truth, but from truth to truth, from lesser truth to higher truth — but it is never from error to truth. If your present state of knowledge is much greater than it was when you were a child, would you look down upon that stage now? Will you look back and call it inanity? Why, your present stage is the knowledge of the child plus something more.

display: Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Way To The Realisation Of A Universal Religion
text: Suppose a man is journeying towards the sun, and as he advances he takes a photograph of the sun at every stage. When he comes back, he has many photographs of the sun, which he places before us. We see that not two are alike, and yet, who will deny that all these are photographs of the same sun, from different standpoints? Take four photographs of this church from different corners: how different they would look, and yet they would all represent this church. In the same way, we are all looking at truth from different standpoints, which vary according to our birth, education, surroundings, and so on. We are viewing truth, getting as much of it as these circumstances will permit, colouring the truth with our own heart, understanding it with our own intellect, and grasping it with our own mind. We can only know as much of truth as is related to us, as much of it as we are able to receive. This makes the difference between man and man, and occasions sometimes even contradictory ideas; yet we all belong to the same great universal truth.
note: Different perspectives on the same truth

He who brought the cup has the water in the form of a cup; he who brought the jar — his water is in the shape of a jar, and so forth; but, in every case, water, and nothing but water, is in the vessel. So it is in the case of religion; our minds are like these vessels, and each one of us is trying to arrive at the realisation of God. God is like that water filling these different vessels, and in each vessel the vision of God comes in the form of the vessel. Yet He is One.

text: All misery and pain come from attachment. I want to do work, I want to do good to a human being; and it is ninety to one that that human being whom I have helped will prove ungrateful and go against me; and the result to me is pain. Karma-Yoga teaches us how to work for work’s sake, unattached, without caring who is helped, and what for. The Karma-Yogi works because it is his nature, because he feels that it is good for him to do so, and he has no object beyond that. His position in this world is that of a giver, and he never cares to receive anything. He knows that he is giving, and does not ask for anything in return and, therefore, he eludes the grasp of misery.

display: Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Way To The Realisation Of A Universal Religion
text: Upon the same tree there are two birds, one on the top, the other below. The one on the top is calm, silent, and majestic, immersed in his own glory; the one on the lower branches, eating sweet and bitter fruits by turns, hopping from branch to branch, is becoming happy and miserable by turns. After a time the lower bird eats an exceptionally bitter fruit and gets disgustful and looks up and sees the other bird, that wondrous one of golden plumage, who eats neither sweet nor bitter fruit, who is neither happy nor miserable, but calm, Selfcentred, and sees nothing beyond his Self. The lower bird longs for this condition but soon forgets it, and again begins to eat the fruits. In a little while, he eats another exceptionally bitter fruit, which makes him feel miserable, and he again looks up, and tries to get nearer to the upper bird. Once more he forgets and after a time he looks up, and so on he goes again and again, until he comes very near to the beautiful bird and sees the reflection of light from his plumage playing around his own body, and he feels a change and seems to melt away; still nearer he comes, and everything about him melts away, and at last he understands this wonderful change. The lower bird was, as it were, only the substantial-looking shadow, the reflection of the higher; he himself was in essence the upper bird all the time. This eating of fruits, sweet and bitter, this lower, little bird, weeping and happy by turns, was a vain chimera, a dream: all along, the real bird was there above, calm and silent, glorious and majestic, beyond grief, beyond sorrow. The upper bird is God, the Lord of this universe; and the lower bird is the human soul, eating the sweet and bitter fruits of this world.
note: Ups and downs of life; finding the calm true self

tags.when_helps: Someone tossed between happiness and misery, longing for a steadier self beyond both.

display_text: Upon the same tree there are two birds, one on the top, the other below. The one on the top is calm, silent, and majestic, immersed in his own glory; the one on the lower branches, eating sweet and bitter fruits by turns, hopping from branch to branch, is becoming happy and miserable by turns. After a time the lower bird eats an exceptionally bitter fruit and gets disgustful and looks up and sees the other bird, that wondrous one of golden plumage, who eats neither sweet nor bitter fruit, who is neither happy nor miserable, but calm, Selfcentred, and sees nothing beyond his Self. The lower bird longs for this condition but soon forgets it, and again begins to eat the fruits. In a little while, he eats another exceptionally bitter fruit, which makes him feel miserable, and he again looks up, and tries to get nearer to the upper bird. Once more he forgets and after a time he looks up, and so on he goes again and again, until he comes very near to the beautiful bird and sees the reflection of light from his plumage playing around his own body, and he feels a change and seems to melt away; still nearer he comes, and everything about him melts away, and at last he understands this wonderful change. The lower bird was, as it were, only the substantial-looking shadow, the reflection of the higher; he himself was in essence the upper bird all the time. This eating of fruits, sweet and bitter, this lower, little bird, weeping and happy by turns, was a vain chimera, a dream: all along, the real bird was there above, calm and silent, glorious and majestic, beyond grief, beyond sorrow. The upper bird is God, the Lord of this universe; and the lower bird is the human soul, eating the sweet and bitter fruits of this world.
plain: A lower bird, happy and miserable by turns among sweet and bitter fruits, keeps nearing a calm golden bird above until it finds it was that bird all along. The upper bird is God; the lower, the soul.
core_idea: The suffering self is really the calm divine Self.

plain_judge.issue: Heavily compressed; loses the lower bird as mere shadow or dream of the upper.

text: In practical daily life we are hurt by small things; we are enslaved by little beings. Misery comes because we think we are finite — we are little beings. text: Many times I have been in the jaws of death, starving, footsore, and weary; for days and days I had had no food, and often could walk no farther; I would sink down under a tree, and life would seem ebbing away. display: Inspired Talks
text: The bullock in the oil-mill never reaches the wisp of hay tied in front of him, he only grinds out the oil. So we chase the will-o’-the-wisp of happiness that always eludes us, and we only grind nature’s mill, then die, merely to begin again. If we could get rid of evil, we should never catch a glimpse of anything higher; we would be satisfied and never struggle to get free. When man finds that all search for happiness in matter is nonsense, then religion begins.
note: chasing happiness that always eludes us

tags.when_helps: Someone chasing happiness that always eludes them, realising the search in material things never satisfies.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: If we examine our own lives, we find that the greatest cause of sorrow is this: we take up something, and put our whole energy on it — perhaps it is a failure and yet we cannot give it up. We know that it is hurting us, that any further clinging to it is simply bringing misery on us; still, we cannot tear ourselves away from it. The bee came to sip the honey, but its feet stuck to the honey-pot and it could not get away.
note: Unable to let go of something that hurts

situations: loss of a dream or plan
tags.when_helps: Someone unable to let go of a failing project or relationship that is hurting them.

display_text: If we examine our own lives, we find that the greatest cause of sorrow is this: we take up something, and put our whole energy on it — perhaps it is a failure and yet we cannot give it up. plain: Our greatest sorrow comes when we pour our energy into something that fails, know it hurts us, and still cannot let go. Like the bee that came for honey, our feet stick to the pot.
core_idea: We suffer by clinging to what hurts us.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: There are men who are never attracted by anything. They can never love, they are hard-hearted and apathetic; they escape most of the miseries of life. tags.when_helps: Someone hurt by love and tempted to harden their heart, reminded that feeling is better than being a wall.

display_text: There are men who are never attracted by anything. They can never love, they are hard-hearted and apathetic; they escape most of the miseries of life. plain: Cold, unloving people escape most of life's miseries, but so does a wall, which never loves or hurts and is still only a wall. Better to be attached and caught than to be a wall.
core_idea: Better to love and suffer than feel nothing.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: We are all beggars. Whatever we do, we want a return. We are all traders. We are traders in life, we are traders in virtue, we are traders in religion. And alas! we are also traders in love.

display_text: We are all beggars. Whatever we do, we want a return. We are all traders. We are traders in life, we are traders in virtue, we are traders in religion. And alas! we are also traders in love.
plain: We are all beggars, wanting a return for whatever we do. We are traders in life, in virtue, in religion, and sadly even in love.
core_idea: We even turn love into a trade.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: We get caught. How? Not by what we give, but by what we expect. We get misery in return for our love; not from the fact that we love, but from the fact that we want love in return. There is no misery where there is no want. Desire, want, is the father of all misery. Desires are bound by the laws of success and failure. Desires must bring misery.
note: Hurt from unreturned love; expectations

tags.when_helps: Someone hurting because their love is not returned, seeing how expectation, not love, causes the pain.

display_text: We get caught. How? Not by what we give, but by what we expect. We get misery in return for our love; not from the fact that we love, but from the fact that we want love in return. There is no misery where there is no want. Desire, want, is the father of all misery. Desires are bound by the laws of success and failure. Desires must bring misery.
plain: We get caught not by what we give but by what we expect: love brings misery only because we want love back. Without wanting there is no misery; desire is the father of all misery.
core_idea: Expecting return, not loving, brings misery.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: Ask nothing; want nothing in return. tags.when_helps: Someone tired of giving without return, invited to give freely and let go of expecting repayment.

display_text: Ask nothing; want nothing in return. plain: Give what you have and want nothing back; it will return a thousandfold, but do not think of that. All of life is giving, and nature will force you to give, so give willingly.
core_idea: Life is giving; give willingly, expecting nothing.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: Even if our every attempt is a failure, and we bleed and are torn asunder, yet, through all this, we have to preserve our heart — we must assert our Godhead in the midst of all these difficulties. Then it requires a superdivine power not to hit back, to keep control, to be unattached.

display_text: Even if our every attempt is a failure, and we bleed and are torn asunder, yet, through all this, we have to preserve our heart — we must assert our Godhead in the midst of all these difficulties. core_idea: Not striking back takes the greatest strength.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: Every day we renew our determination to be unattached. We cast our eyes back and look at the past objects of our love and attachment, and feel how every one of them made us miserable. We went down into the depths of despondency because of our “love”! We found ourselves mere slaves in the hands of others, we were dragged down and down! And we make a fresh determination: “Henceforth, I will be master of myself; henceforth, I will have control over myself.” But the time comes, and the same story once more! Again the soul is caught and cannot get out. The bird is in a net, struggling and fluttering.
note: Repeating the same painful patterns despite resolve

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps resolving to break free of attachments and keeps falling back, feeling understood in the struggle.

display_text: Every day we renew our determination to be unattached. We cast our eyes back and look at the past objects of our love and attachment, and feel how every one of them made us miserable. We went down into the depths of despondency because of our “love”! We found ourselves mere slaves in the hands of others, we were dragged down and down! And we make a fresh determination: “Henceforth, I will be master of myself; henceforth, I will have control over myself.” But the time comes, and the same story once more! plain: Every day we resolve to be unattached, remembering how each attachment made us miserable and enslaved, and we vow to master ourselves. Then the same story repeats, and the soul is caught again, like a bird struggling in a net.
core_idea: We vow freedom, then get caught again.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: I know the difficulties. Tremendous they are, and ninety per cent of us become discouraged and lose heart, and in our turn, often become pessimists and cease to believe in sincerity, love, and all that is grand and noble. So, we find men who in the freshness of their lives have been forgiving, kind, simple, and guileless, become in old age lying masks of men.
note: Becoming cynical and discouraged with age

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling hardships turning them cynical, recognising that danger and resolving to keep their heart open.

display_text: I know the difficulties. plain: The difficulties are huge; most of us lose heart, turn pessimist and stop believing in sincerity, love and everything noble. So people who were kind, simple and forgiving when young become lying masks in old age.
core_idea: Discouragement can turn the kind into cynics.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: Analyse yourselves and you will find that every blow you have received, came to you because you prepared yourselves for it. You did half, and the external world did the other half: that is how the blow came. That will sober us down. At the same time, from this very analysis will come a note of hope, and the note of hope is: “I have no control of the external world, but that which is in me and nearer unto me, my own world, is in my control. If the two together are required to make a failure, if the two together are necessary to give me a blow, I will not contribute the one which is in my keeping; and how then can the blow come? If I get real control of myself, the blow will never come.”
note: Taking responsibility for one's part in setbacks

tags.when_helps: Someone repeatedly hurt by life, finding sober hope in what remains within their own control.

display_text: Analyse yourselves and you will find that every blow you have received, came to you because you prepared yourselves for it. plain: Every blow you receive needs your half as well as the world's. You cannot control the world, but you can control your own half, and if you truly master yourself, the blow will never come.
core_idea: Control your part and the blow cannot land.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: We are all the time, from our childhood, trying to lay the blame upon something outside ourselves. We are always standing up to set right other people, and not ourselves. If we are miserable, we say, “Oh, the world is a devil’s world.” We curse others and say, “What infatuated fools!” But why should we be in such a world, if we really are so good? If this is a devil’s world, we must be devils also; why else should we be here? “Oh, the people of the world are so selfish!” True enough; but why should we be found in that company, if we be better?
note: Blaming others and the world for unhappiness

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone blaming a selfish world for their misery, challenged to examine their own part.

display_text: We are all the time, from our childhood, trying to lay the blame upon something outside ourselves. We are always standing up to set right other people, and not ourselves. display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: We are to take care of ourselves — that much we can do — and give up attending to others for a time. Let us perfect the means; the end will take care of itself. tags.when_helps: Someone overwhelmed trying to fix others or the world, reminded to tend first to their own life.

display_text: We are to take care of ourselves — that much we can do — and give up attending to others for a time. Let us perfect the means; the end will take care of itself. plain: Take care of yourself and stop attending to others for a while; perfect the means and the end will follow. The world can be good and pure only if our lives are, so let us purify ourselves.
core_idea: Purify yourself and the world follows.

text: We complain of others in our failures. The moment I am unsuccessful, I say, so-and-so is the cause of the failure. In failure, one does not like to confess one’s own faults and weaknesses. display_text: We complain of others in our failures. The moment I am unsuccessful, I say, so-and-so is the cause of the failure. core_idea: In failure we blame others, not ourselves.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): The Powers of the Mind
text: There is a little bubble coming from the bottom of a lake; we do not see it coming all the time, we see it only when it bursts on the surface; so, we can perceive thoughts only after they develop a great deal, or after they become actions. We constantly complain that we have no control over our actions, over our thoughts. But how can we have it? If we can get control over the fine movements, if we can get hold of thought at the root, before it has become thought, before it has become action, then it would be possible for us to control the whole.
note: Feeling unable to control one's thoughts and actions

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break

display_text: There is a little bubble coming from the bottom of a lake; we do not see it coming all the time, we see it only when it bursts on the surface; so, we can perceive thoughts only after they develop a great deal, or after they become actions. display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): The Powers of the Mind
text: And what an amount of attention does business require, and what a rigorous taskmaster it is! Even if the father, the mother, the wife, or the child dies, business cannot stop! This science calls for more application than any business can ever require. Many men can succeed in business; very few in this.
note: Having to keep working while grieving

tags.when_helps: Someone forced back to work while grieving or heartbroken, feeling the harshness of that demand named.

display_text: And what an amount of attention does business require, and what a rigorous taskmaster it is! Even if the father, the mother, the wife, or the child dies, business cannot stop! display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Hints On Practical Spirituality
text: When I was a boy, I used to criticise the ascetic practices of my countrymen; great preachers in our own land have criticised them; the greatest man that was ever born, Buddha himself, criticised them. But all the same, as I am growing older, I feel that I have no right to judge. Sometimes I wish that, in spite of all their incongruities, I had one fragment of their power to do and suffer. Often I think that my judgment and my criticism do not proceed from any dislike of torture, but from sheer cowardice — because I cannot do it — I dare not do it.
note: Growing humbler about judging others

display_text: When I was a boy, I used to criticise the ascetic practices of my countrymen; great preachers in our own land have criticised them; the greatest man that was ever born, Buddha himself, criticised them. Similarly, external things furnish us with suggestions, over which we project our own ideals and make our objects. The wicked see this world as a perfect hell, and the good as a perfect heaven. Lovers see this world as full of love, and haters as full of hatred; fighters see nothing but strife, and the peaceful nothing but peace.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. III): The Free Soul
text: I was once travelling in the desert in India. I travelled for over a month and always found the most beautiful landscapes before me, beautiful lakes and all that. One day I was very thirsty and I wanted to have a drink at one of these lakes; but when I approached that lake it vanished. Immediately with a blow came into my brain the idea that this was a mirage about which I had read all my life; and then I remembered and smiled at my folly, that for the last month all the beautiful landscapes and lakes I had been seeing were this mirage, but I could not distinguish them then. The next morning I again began my march; there was the lake and the landscape, but with it immediately came the idea, “This is a mirage.” Once known it had lost its power of illusion. So this illusion of the universe will break one day.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. III): One Existence Appearing As Many

plain: A perfect person sees perfection in others. When someone sees imperfection, it is their own mind projecting it; how could they see it if it were not in them?
core_idea: The imperfection we see in others is our own

display: Lectures from Colombo to Almora: First Public Lecture In The East
text: Individuals have each their own peculiarities, and each man has his own method of growth, his own life marked out for him by the infinite past life, by all his past Karma as we Hindus say. note: Finding one's own path; the present shapes the future

core_idea: The past shapes us; the present shapes the future

display: Lectures from Colombo to Almora: First Public Lecture In The East
text: “As the different rivers, taking their start from different mountains, running straight or crooked, at last come unto the ocean, so, O Shiva, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead unto These.” Though they may take various roads, all are on the ways.
